facts.title: shell=True turns interpolated data into shell syntax
facts.fact: subprocess.run(..., shell=True) hands the complete command string to /bin/sh -c, so the shell parses quotes, semicolons, backticks, dollar expansion and redirections after Python has finished building the string. Any value interpolated into that string is therefore reachable as shell syntax rather than as an opaque argument. The list form with shell=False calls execve directly, so every element becomes exactly one argv entry and no shell exists to reinterpret metacharacters.
details: On POSIX, shell=True always means /bin/sh -c; it is not a portability switch.
A single string passed with shell=False is interpreted as a program path, not as a command line.
check=True raises CalledProcessError instead of silently discarding a non-zero exit status.
Arguments are world-readable in the process table, so pass secrets over stdin or an inherited file descriptor.
shlex.quote is a last resort for the rare case where a real shell pipeline cannot be avoided.
pitfalls: Assuming that manually wrapping a value in quotes makes shell=True safe; quoting rules are context dependent.
Concatenating a fixed command with a variable and passing the result as one list element.

code.secure:
import subprocess


def render(name: str) -> None:
    subprocess.run(
        ["convert", name, "/srv/out/preview.png"],
        shell=False,
        check=True,
    )
code.issue: shell=True re-parses the interpolated filename, so shell metacharacters inside name become syntax. The list form with shell=False passes name as one argv element.

mcqs.question: A function builds a command with an f-string and calls subprocess.run with shell=True. Which change removes the command-injection risk while running the same program?
options: Keep shell=True and wrap the value in single quotes
Pass a list of arguments with shell=False
Add check=True to the existing call
Encode the value with base64 before interpolation
mcqs.rationale: With shell=False the operating system receives an argv array and no shell parses the value. Quoting, check=True and encoding do not remove the shell from the path.

facts.title: Joining a base directory with user input does not confine the result
facts.fact: pathlib's / operator and os.path.join both discard the earlier components when a later component is absolute, so Path('/srv/reports') / '/etc/passwd' resolves to /etc/passwd. A relative component containing ../ segments also escapes the base after normalisation. Confinement requires resolving the candidate and then proving that it is still inside the resolved base, for example with Path.is_relative_to on Python 3.9 or later, or by comparing os.path.commonpath results.
details: resolve() follows symlinks, which is what you want when the real target must stay inside the base.
is_relative_to compares path components, so /srv/reports-backup is not treated as inside /srv/reports.
os.path.commonpath raises ValueError when the paths are on different drives on Windows.
Decode URL or form input before the check, and check after every transformation, not before.
Python 3.12 added Path.walk and 3.13 tightened some path semantics; pin behaviour to the interpreter you deploy.
pitfalls: Checking for the substring '..' instead of resolving and comparing the final path.
Validating the raw string, then calling resolve() later in a different function.

code.issue: An absolute name replaces BASE and ../ segments climb out of it. The secure form resolves the candidate and rejects anything outside the resolved base.

mcqs.question: BASE is Path('/srv/reports') and name is attacker-controlled. Why is (BASE / name).read_bytes() unsafe?
options: Path division rejects absolute paths but not symlinks
An absolute name discards BASE, and ../ segments can escape it
read_bytes only follows relative symlinks
Python normalises .. before joining, so the base always wins
mcqs.rationale: The / operator follows os.path.join semantics: an absolute right-hand side replaces the left-hand side, and relative traversal segments are collapsed during resolution. Confinement needs an explicit containment check.

facts.title: Unpickling untrusted bytes is code execution by design
facts.fact: The pickle format is a stack language that can name and call arbitrary globals through the REDUCE opcode, so a crafted stream can invoke any importable callable when the object is reconstructed. There is no restricted mode that makes loads() safe for hostile input: a find_class allowlist narrows the gadget set, but any permitted class with a dangerous __reduce__ can still be abused, so authenticity has to be established before unpickling. Use a data-only format such as JSON with explicit schema validation, and treat pickle as a trusted internal serialisation format at most.
details: Pickle is documented as not secure against erroneous or maliciously constructed data.
If pickle must cross a boundary, sign the bytes with HMAC and verify before calling loads().
The same concern applies to shelve, multiprocessing over a network socket, and pandas.read_pickle.
JSON has no object graph, so __reduce__ has nothing to invoke, but you still need type and size validation.
YAML and marshal have their own unsafe constructors; a safe format is a decision, not a library property.
pitfalls: Believing that a private network or an internal queue makes pickle input trustworthy.
Adding a custom Unpickler.find_class allowlist and assuming it neutralises every gadget.

code.issue: pickle.loads executes whatever the stream tells it to import and call. The secure version uses a data-only format and rejects unexpected keys instead of reconstructing objects.

mcqs.question: Which statement about pickle.loads on data received from a network peer is correct?
options: It is safe if the peer uses the same Python version
It is safe when the payload is compressed first
It can invoke arbitrary importable callables, so the input must be trusted or authenticated
It only constructs built-in container types
mcqs.rationale: The pickle VM can resolve globals and call them during reconstruction. Version or compression does not constrain that, and the format is explicitly documented as unsafe for untrusted data.

misconceptions.claim: Pickle is fine on an internal network because only our services can reach it.
misconceptions.correction: Network position is not an authentication mechanism. Any SSRF, compromised peer, or misrouted message becomes remote code execution; sign the payload and verify before unpickling, or switch to a data-only format.

facts.title: yaml.load with an unsafe loader constructs Python objects
facts.fact: PyYAML tags such as !!python/object/apply let a document request construction of arbitrary Python objects, and the unsafe loaders honour those tags while parsing. yaml.safe_load restricts the document to standard YAML types and rejects unknown tags, which is the correct default for configuration that arrives from users, plugins, or the network. Explicitly selecting SafeLoader is clearer than relying on a library default that has changed between releases.
details: PyYAML 6.0 made the Loader argument mandatory for yaml.load; FullLoader supports a wider tag set than SafeLoader and is not the right choice for hostile input.
safe_load supports anchors, aliases, and merge keys, so ordinary configuration files keep working.
Alias expansion is unbounded, so a small document can still exhaust memory; cap input size and alias count.
ruamel.yaml users should call YAML(typ='safe') rather than the round-trip loader for untrusted input.
Validating the resulting structure against a schema is a separate step from choosing a safe loader.
pitfalls: Passing Loader=yaml.FullLoader because it sounds safer than Loader.
Assuming base64 or a signature removes the need for a safe loader.

code.issue: The unsafe loader honours python/object tags and can construct arbitrary objects. safe_load resolves only standard YAML types and the explicit type check rejects surprising documents.

mcqs.question: Which PyYAML call avoids constructing arbitrary Python objects from an untrusted document?
options: yaml.load(text, Loader=yaml.Loader)
yaml.load(text, Loader=yaml.FullLoader)
yaml.safe_load(text)
yaml.load(text)
mcqs.rationale: safe_load uses SafeLoader, which recognises only standard YAML types and raises on python/object tags. The unsafe Loader permits object construction, FullLoader goes beyond SafeLoader, and yaml.load requires an explicit loader in PyYAML 6.

misconceptions.claim: safe_load is too limited for real configuration because it disables anchors and aliases.
misconceptions.correction: SafeLoader keeps anchors, aliases, and merge keys; it removes Python object tags and other executable constructors. Teams that hit limits are usually relying on custom tags that should be modelled as plain data.

facts.title: eval and exec execute strings with the full power of the interpreter
facts.fact: eval compiles and runs an expression in the current process, with access to builtins unless they are removed, and exec does the same for statements. Removing __builtins__ is not a sandbox because attribute traversal can recover object, subclasses, and imports. For literal data use ast.literal_eval, which parses and returns only Python literals; for a small expression language, parse with ast and walk an explicit node allowlist so unknown syntax is rejected before anything is evaluated.
details: ast.literal_eval rejects calls, attribute access, and comprehensions, so it cannot run code.
A node allowlist must reject every node type it did not explicitly handle, not just the dangerous ones it knows.
eval also defeats static analysis and coverage, so the code path is rarely reviewed.
For arithmetic rules consider a real expression library with a documented, non-Turing-complete grammar.
compile() plus exec has the same trust properties; a separate interpreter process is the only strong isolation.
pitfalls: Deleting __builtins__ and calling the result a sandbox.
Using eval for type conversion when int(), float(), or json.loads already parse the input.

code.vulnerable:
def total(expression: str) -> float:
    return eval(expression)
code.issue: eval runs whatever expression it receives. The secure form parses the text, accepts only a binary arithmetic node with literal numeric operands, and evaluates it with a fixed operator table.

mcqs.question: What is the safest replacement when the goal is to read a Python literal such as a list or dict from text?
options: eval(text, {'__builtins__': {}})
ast.literal_eval(text)
exec(text) with an empty namespace
compile(text, '<input>', 'eval')
mcqs.rationale: ast.literal_eval parses the text and returns only literal structures; it never executes calls or attribute access. Empty builtins, exec, and compile all retain code-execution paths.

references.title: CWE-95: Improper Neutralization of Directives in Dynamically Evaluated Code

facts.title: Parameter placeholders keep values out of the SQL grammar
facts.fact: A DB-API driver sends the statement text and the bound values separately, so the database parses the statement once and then substitutes values as data. Building the statement with an f-string or % formatting merges data into the grammar, where a quote can end a literal and the remainder is parsed as SQL. Placeholders differ by driver (? for sqlite3 and MySQL, %s for psycopg, :name or $1 elsewhere), but the principle is the same: never format values into statement text.
details: executemany with a list of parameter tuples reuses one parsed statement for bulk work.
Parameters cannot represent table or column names, ASC/DESC, or SQL keywords; those need an allowlist.
Driver-side escaping is not equivalent, because it depends on connection charset and SQL mode.
Some drivers let you pass parameters positionally or by mapping; match the placeholder style exactly.
Turn on the database's statement log in development to see whether values arrive separately.
pitfalls: Using a parameter placeholder inside a quoted string literal, which makes it a literal question mark.
Assuming an ORM removes injection risk when raw() or text() fragments are used.

code.issue: The f-string lets a quote in email close the literal and append new SQL syntax. The placeholder version binds email as a value after the statement has been parsed.

mcqs.question: Why can a bound parameter not be used to choose the column in ORDER BY?
options: Drivers reject strings longer than the column name
Parameters are bound as values, and an identifier is part of the statement grammar
ORDER BY is always executed before parameters are bound
It is allowed, but only with $1 style placeholders
mcqs.rationale: Binding substitutes a value into a slot the parser has already resolved; identifiers, keywords, and sort direction change the parse tree, so they must come from a fixed allowlist instead.

references.title: sqlite3 - Passing parameters to SQL statements

facts.title: Predictable temporary filenames create symlink and race windows
facts.fact: A name such as /tmp/report.$$ can be predicted or read from the process table, so another local user can pre-create a symlink at that path and redirect the privileged writer onto a file they choose. tempfile.mkstemp asks the kernel for a fresh name, creates it with O_CREAT|O_EXCL and mode 0600, and returns an open descriptor plus the path, which removes both the prediction and the create-if-absent race. Treat the returned path as sensitive and remove it with a finally block or an EXIT trap.
details: NamedTemporaryFile(delete=False) is convenient but leaves cleanup to you and follows platform-specific rename rules.
Use dir= to place temporary files on the same filesystem as the final destination when atomic rename is required.
The descriptor from mkstemp should be wrapped with os.fdopen; opening the path again reintroduces a race.
A sticky bit on /tmp prevents deletion of other users' files but does not prevent a symlink being planted at a guessed name.
On Windows, mkstemp still opens exclusively, but file sharing and deletion semantics differ from POSIX.
pitfalls: Calling os.path.exists before opening a temp path, which is a time-of-check to time-of-use gap.
Using the shell's $$ or $RANDOM as the only source of uniqueness.

code.vulnerable:
PATH = "/tmp/report-worker.tmp"


def write_report(payload: bytes) -> None:
    with open(PATH, "wb") as handle:
        handle.write(payload)
code.secure:
import os
import tempfile


def write_report(payload: bytes) -> str:
    fd, path = tempfile.mkstemp(prefix="report-", suffix=".tmp", dir="/srv/scratch")
    try:
        with os.fdopen(fd, "wb") as handle:
            handle.write(payload)
    except BaseException:
        os.unlink(path)
        raise
    return path
code.issue: The fixed path can be pre-created as a symlink by another local user. mkstemp creates a new file with O_EXCL and 0600 and returns the descriptor, eliminating the prediction and the race.

mcqs.question: Which property of tempfile.mkstemp removes the symlink attack on a shared /tmp?
options: It stores the file under a randomly named directory
It creates the file with O_CREAT|O_EXCL, so an existing path is never followed or reused
It encrypts the file contents with a per-process key
It automatically deletes the file when the process exits
mcqs.rationale: Exclusive creation makes the kernel fail if the name already exists, so a planted symlink cannot be opened as the target. Cleanup and permissions are separate properties.

facts.title: Security tokens need an OS CSPRNG and a comparison that does not leak
facts.fact: The random module implements a Mersenne Twister, a deterministic generator whose internal state can be reconstructed from a few hundred outputs, so it must never produce passwords, reset tokens, session identifiers, or salts. The secrets module reads from the operating system CSPRNG and provides token_urlsafe, token_hex, and compare_digest. String equality returns as soon as two values differ, which leaks a timing signal about the matching prefix; hmac.compare_digest is written to take the same time regardless of where the mismatch occurs.
details: random.seed with a timestamp or PID is guessable and does not repair the generator's predictability.
secrets.compare_digest is the same function as hmac.compare_digest and works on ASCII str or bytes.
Compare bytes when the value is not ASCII, because str comparison raises on non-ASCII input.
Timing differences are usually small, so treat constant-time comparison as one layer, not the only control.
Token length should come from entropy requirements (secrets.token_bytes(32)), not from a character count chosen for looks.
pitfalls: Seeding random with time.time() and believing that makes it unpredictable.
Hashing a password with a single fast SHA-256 round instead of a password KDF such as scrypt or Argon2.

code.issue: random is a deterministic PRNG, and == exits at the first differing character. secrets draws from the OS CSPRNG, and compare_digest avoids early-exit timing differences.

mcqs.question: Which function should generate a password-reset token?
options: random.randint(0, 10**16)
secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
hashlib.md5(str(time.time()).encode()).hexdigest()
uuid.uuid4().int
mcqs.rationale: secrets reads from the operating system CSPRNG. random is predictable, hashing a timestamp inherits the timestamp's entropy, and uuid4 is not specified for security tokens even when it uses good randomness.

misconceptions.claim: Using == for an API token check is fine because the comparison happens on the server.
misconceptions.correction: Server-side comparison still returns early on a mismatch, and enough measurements can reveal the matching prefix. Use hmac.compare_digest for secrets that an attacker can submit repeatedly.

facts.title: A virtual environment isolates packages, not privileges
facts.fact: python -m venv gives a project its own site-packages directory and interpreter links, but code installed into it still runs with the invoking user's permissions, including at install time. Modern build backends execute arbitrary code from an sdist or a malicious wheel's build step, and pip resolves names against an index whose contents can change. Reproducible, verifiable installs combine a lockfile, hashes for every artifact (--require-hashes), a restricted index, and an audit step that compares resolved versions with advisory data.
details: pip install --require-hashes refuses any requirement without a matching SHA-256 digest, which pins the artifact and not just the version.
A wheel installs as-is; an sdist runs its build backend, so source distributions carry more install-time risk.
pip-audit queries advisory databases for the resolved environment; run it in CI as well as locally.
Constraint files pin transitive versions, while a lockfile records the exact artifacts that were resolved.
Index configuration can be overridden by environment variables, so check pip config debug in CI.
Installing with --no-deps avoids surprise transitive additions only if you already manage the full set.
pitfalls: Assuming a venv contains an untrusted package's damage to the project directory.
Pinning top-level packages without pinning or hashing transitive dependencies.

commands.purpose: Create an isolated interpreter environment for one project.
Install only artifacts whose SHA-256 digests are recorded in the lockfile.
Compare the installed environment against known advisories and fail on findings.
Show which index URLs and environment overrides pip will actually use.

misconceptions.claim: Installing a package into a virtual environment contains any malicious code it carries.
misconceptions.correction: The venv changes module resolution, not the OS security context. Install-time hooks run as your user and can read your SSH keys, CI tokens, and the repository, so treat installation as code execution and use hashes, review, and least-privilege CI runners.

facts.title: Unquoted expansions undergo word splitting and pathname expansion
facts.fact: After parameter expansion, an unquoted $var is split on the characters in IFS and each resulting word is then treated as a glob pattern, so a value containing spaces becomes several arguments and a value containing * expands to matching filenames. Double quotes suppress both steps and keep the value as one argument. "$@" expands to one word per positional parameter and preserves boundaries, while "$*" joins them into a single word using the first character of IFS.
details: Use -- before a filename argument so a value beginning with - is not parsed as an option.
set -f disables pathname expansion for the rest of the shell, but quoting is more local and clearer.
Arrays should be expanded as "${array[@]}"; ${array[@]} without quotes splits again.
Command substitution should be quoted: files=$(find ...) then printf '%s\n' "$files", or better mapfile.
IFS changes are scoped to a command when written as IFS=, read -r a b.
pitfalls: Quoting the variable but leaving a glob or command substitution unquoted on the same line.
Using $* when the script needs to forward its arguments unchanged.

code.secure:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
archive=$1
cp -- "$archive" /srv/backup/
code.issue: The unquoted archive is split and globbed before cp sees it, so a filename with spaces becomes several arguments and a leading dash can be read as an option. Quoting and -- keep it one operand.

mcqs.question: A script runs cp $src /srv/backup/. Which input demonstrates the word-splitting bug?
options: src='report.txt'
src='quarterly report.txt'
src='report-2026.txt'
src='./report.txt'
mcqs.rationale: The space is in IFS, so the unquoted expansion produces two arguments, 'quarterly' and 'report.txt'. Quoting "$src" passes the single filename through unchanged.

facts.title: set -euo pipefail is a useful baseline with documented exceptions
facts.fact: set -e exits on an unchecked failing command, but the shell deliberately ignores failures in conditions (if, while, until), in any command of an && or || list except the last, and after !. The u option turns unset variable expansion into an error, and pipefail makes a pipeline return the rightmost non-zero status. None of this is a substitute for explicit error handling: arithmetic commands return a status derived from their value, so ((count++)) returns 1 when the previous value was 0 and can terminate the script under -e.
details: local out=$(false) returns the status of local, not of the command substitution, so the failure is hidden.
With pipefail, producer | head can exit 141 because the producer receives SIGPIPE when head closes early.
A command that must be allowed to fail belongs in an explicit if ! cmd; then ... fi.
Settings do not propagate into subshells created by command substitution, so set them inside functions that run there.
set -u does not catch unset array elements in every bash version; test the behaviour you depend on.
pitfalls: Believing that set -e makes a script fail-safe, then shipping a pipeline whose middle stage is unchecked.
Using set -e in an interactive shell and losing the session on a failed command.

code.vulnerable:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
count=0
while read -r line; do
  ((count++))
done < <(printf 'a\nb\n')
echo "$count"
code.secure:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
count=0
while read -r line; do
  count=$((count + 1))
done < <(printf 'a\nb\n')
echo "$count"
code.issue: ((count++)) evaluates to 0 on the first iteration and therefore returns status 1, which -e treats as a failure and exits the loop. The assignment form always returns success.

mcqs.question: Under set -e, which construct still runs a failing command without exiting the script?
options: A bare command on its own line
The left side of || in cmd || fallback
The last command of a pipeline without pipefail
A command inside a function called on its own line
mcqs.rationale: The shell exempts any command in an && or || list except the final one, and the same applies to conditions and negated commands. Functions called normally and pipeline members (without pipefail) still propagate failure.

misconceptions.claim: Adding set -euo pipefail is enough to make a shell script robust.
misconceptions.correction: The options leave real gaps: masked failures in command substitutions, exempt positions, SIGPIPE statuses, and unset variables that are only conditionally set. Review each external command and handle expected failures explicitly.

references.title: Bash Reference Manual - The Set Builtin
ShellCheck SC2310: set -e is disabled in this function

facts.title: eval reparses its arguments, so data becomes code
facts.fact: eval concatenates its arguments and parses the result as shell source, which means quoting is applied twice: once when the string is built and again when eval reads it. User-controlled text can therefore inject commands, redirections, or variable assignments even if it looked quoted at the call site. Most uses of eval are avoidable: pass arguments directly, store command words in arrays, and use indirect expansion ${!name} or printf -v when the goal is to write a variable.
details: bash -c "$string" and ssh host "$cmd" have the same second-parse property as eval.
Arrays preserve argument boundaries: cmd=(grep -F -- "$pattern" file); "${cmd[@]}".
printf -v var '%s' "$value" assigns without evaluating the value as code.
eval is occasionally legitimate for constructing code from a trusted, fully controlled template.
Because eval hides data flow, static review and shellcheck cannot follow the injected text.
pitfalls: Escaping a value for eval by adding backslashes, then missing a metacharacter.
Using eval to expand a variable whose name is in another variable instead of ${!prefix}.

code.secure:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
pattern=$1
grep -F -- "$pattern" /var/log/app.log
code.issue: eval parses the pattern as part of the command line, so spaces, semicolons, or substitutions change the command. The secure form passes the pattern as a quoted operand to grep.

mcqs.question: What is the main reason eval is dangerous with untrusted input?
options: It runs the command in a subshell and loses environment variables
It applies a second round of parsing, so the value can become syntax
It disables set -u for the rest of the script
It always runs as root
mcqs.rationale: eval builds a string and asks the shell to parse it again, so quoting done when the string was assembled is consumed and any metacharacter in the data is interpreted as shell syntax.

references.title: Bash Reference Manual - Bourne Shell Builtins (eval)

facts.title: mktemp plus umask and a trap is the portable temp-file pattern
facts.fact: A predictable path such as /tmp/job.$$ can be pre-created as a symlink by another local user, and a redirect then writes through it with the script's privileges. mktemp creates a unique name atomically with O_EXCL and mode 0600, and printing the name for command substitution is safe when the call itself is checked. Set umask 077 before creating any adjacent files, and install a trap so the path is removed on both normal exit and signals.
details: mktemp without a template uses TMPDIR or /tmp and creates one file; mktemp -d creates a directory.
Check the command substitution: out=$(mktemp) || exit 1, because a failed mktemp yields an empty name.
trap 'rm -f -- "$out"' EXIT runs on normal exit and on signals that terminate the shell.
Never reuse a temp name across concurrent runs; uniqueness must come from the kernel, not from the PID.
The sticky bit protects existing files in /tmp from deletion by others but does not stop pre-creation of a guessed name.
pitfalls: Using $$ or $RANDOM as the only uniqueness source, which is guessable and can collide after a fork.
Creating the file with mktemp and then reopening the path instead of using the descriptor when one is available.

code.secure:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
umask 077
out=$(mktemp) || exit 1
trap 'rm -f -- "$out"' EXIT
printf 'rows=%s\n' 42 >"$out"
code.issue: The PID-based name is predictable, so another user can plant a symlink and redirect the write. mktemp creates an exclusive 0600 file, umask protects new files, and the trap removes it.

mcqs.question: Why is tmp=$(mktemp) still incomplete without checking the exit status?
options: mktemp can return a directory instead of a file
A failed mktemp leaves tmp empty, and redirections then target an empty path
mktemp prints the name to stderr
The file is created with mode 0644 by default
mcqs.rationale: Command substitution captures stdout regardless of exit status, so a failure yields an empty string. Guarding with || exit 1 prevents later redirections from operating on an unintended path.

facts.title: A writable or relative PATH entry lets another directory supply your commands
facts.fact: Command lookup walks PATH from left to right and runs the first matching executable, so an entry that is writable by another user, a relative entry, or an empty entry (which means the current directory) allows a planted binary to run instead of the intended tool. Scripts inherit PATH from the caller and from rc files, and sudo resets it only when env_reset and secure_path are in effect. Set a fixed, minimal PATH at the top of privileged scripts and invoke tools by absolute path when the environment is not under your control.
details: An empty PATH component means the current working directory, which is especially dangerous in a directory an attacker can write.
sudo's env_reset removes most inherited variables; secure_path then defines the PATH used for the command.
Aliases and shell functions can shadow a command name before PATH is consulted, which matters in interactive shells.
cron and systemd services start with a minimal environment, so relative assumptions often break there first.
Use command -v to see what would run, and type -a to list every match.
pitfalls: Prepending . to PATH for convenience in a shared or privileged account.
Assuming quoting a command name prevents PATH hijacking; quoting affects arguments, not lookup.

commands.purpose: Show each PATH component on its own line so relative or empty entries stand out.
List every command, alias, or function that would satisfy the name, in lookup order.
Run a tool with a fixed minimal PATH to test behaviour without the caller's environment.

misconceptions.claim: Calling a command by name is safe because PATH is controlled by the administrator.
misconceptions.correction: PATH is per-process and inherited from the caller, rc files, CI variables, and service units. A privileged script should set its own PATH or use absolute paths; administrator ownership of the system default does not constrain the environment the script is started with.

references.title: Bash Reference Manual - Command Search and Execution

facts.title: curl piped into a shell executes whatever the server returns at that moment
facts.fact: curl https://host/install.sh | sh streams the response body straight into an interpreter, so the content is executed without being stored or reviewed, and a compromised host, a changed release artifact, or an intercepted connection yields immediate code execution. TLS authenticates the endpoint for this connection, not the bytes you expected, and -k or a redirect to http can remove even that. The safer pattern downloads to a file with --fail, verifies a published digest or signature out of band, inspects the script, and then runs a pinned version.
details: --fail makes curl return an error for HTTP 4xx and 5xx instead of saving an error page as the script.
--proto '=https' disables every protocol except HTTPS; --proto-redir applies a separate restriction to redirects.
A digest fetched from the same server as the artifact proves integrity, not authenticity; compare against a separately published value.
Pin the version and record the digest in configuration so the installer is reproducible.
Piping to sudo sh adds privilege to the same unreviewed content path.
pitfalls: Believing HTTPS alone makes curl | sh safe; the server is still free to serve different code.
Using curl -k to get past a certificate error in a bootstrap script.

commands.purpose: Download an installer to a file, failing on HTTP errors and restricting the protocol.
Compute the digest to compare with a value published through a separate trusted channel.
Read the downloaded script before deciding whether to run it.

mcqs.question: What does HTTPS guarantee about a curl | sh installation?
options: The script cannot contain malicious commands
The bytes are authenticated to the host named in the certificate, not to a known release
The script will run with reduced privileges
The download is reproducible on later dates
mcqs.rationale: TLS authenticates the server for that session. It does not pin the content or the release, so the host can serve different code later or after compromise. Integrity and reproducibility require a digest or signature checked separately.

references.title: CWE-494: Download of Code Without Integrity Check

facts.title: A sudoers command rule is a prefix match, not a sandbox
facts.fact: sudo compares the command line against the rule and, unless a digest or exact restriction is used, permits additional arguments, so a rule for /usr/bin/systemctl restart app may also allow restarting another unit or passing options that load attacker-controlled content. Many permitted programs can spawn a shell or write files by design (editors, pagers, find -exec, tar with checkpoint actions, package managers, interpreters), which turns delegated administration into full root. Rules should name exact binaries with fixed arguments where possible, avoid NOPASSWD for shell-capable tools, and keep env_reset enabled so LD_PRELOAD, PYTHONPATH, and similar variables are not inherited.
details: sudo -l shows the effective rules for the invoking user, including whether a password is required.
visudo -c checks syntax before the file is installed, which prevents locking yourself out.
Wildcards in sudoers match across spaces and slashes, so they rarely express the restriction people expect.
The SETENV tag and env_keep can reintroduce environment-based privilege escalation.
sudoedit restricts editing to files the user could already write, which is safer than granting an editor.
Command digests (sha256) pin the binary but not its configuration or the files it reads.
pitfalls: Granting NOPASSWD on a script that reads a file from a user-writable directory.
Assuming a full path in sudoers makes argument injection impossible.

commands.purpose: Show the sudo rules that apply to the current user and whether a password is required.
Validate sudoers syntax before relying on the edited file.

misconceptions.claim: Listing a binary by absolute path in sudoers means the user can only run that exact command.
misconceptions.correction: Unless the rule pins arguments, sudo permits extra arguments, and many binaries can execute other programs or write arbitrary files. Delegation is only as narrow as the least powerful thing the permitted program can be made to do.

facts.title: Execution policy is a safety setting; language mode and application control are the boundary
facts.fact: Microsoft's own documentation states that execution policy is not a security boundary: it helps prevent accidental script execution, and any user can bypass it with -ExecutionPolicy Bypass, by reading the file and invoking its content, or by using another host. The controls that actually constrain code are Constrained Language Mode, which removes arbitrary .NET type access and Add-Type from the session, and application control such as AppLocker or WDAC, which decides what may execute at all. Treat a bypassed policy as expected and design detection and least privilege around the real controls.
details: LanguageMode can be FullLanguage, ConstrainedLanguage, or Restricted; CLM is enforced through AppLocker/WDAC policy or the __PSLockdownPolicy environment variable.
Under CLM, cmdlets still run but method invocation on arbitrary types, Add-Type, and many COM objects are blocked.
Script block logging records the text PowerShell compiles, including content that was decoded or downloaded, in event ID 4104.
AppLocker default rules are permissive; only explicitly enforced collections restrict execution.
Signing plus an AllSigned policy gives integrity for reviewed scripts, but it is still a policy setting that a caller can override.
pitfalls: Reporting that a host is protected because Get-ExecutionPolicy returns RemoteSigned.
Assuming CLM blocks all risky cmdlets; it constrains the language, not the intent of allowed commands.

commands.purpose: Show the effective policy for each scope rather than only the most specific one.
Report whether the current session is FullLanguage or ConstrainedLanguage.
Inspect the application control rules that are actually enforced on the host.

mcqs.question: What does setting execution policy to AllSigned reliably prevent?
options: Any unsigned PowerShell code from running on the machine
Accidental execution of unsigned scripts through normal script invocation
PowerShell from being used by an administrator
Decoded commands passed with -EncodedCommand
mcqs.rationale: AllSigned changes the default behaviour of script invocation for hosts that honour the policy. It is not a security boundary: callers can bypass it, and content can be read and executed through other paths.

misconceptions.claim: A locked-down execution policy stops malware that uses PowerShell.
misconceptions.correction: Attackers routinely run with -ExecutionPolicy Bypass, -EncodedCommand, or by loading script text directly. Detection depends on script block logging, AMSI, and application control, and prevention depends on WDAC/AppLocker plus least privilege.

facts.title: EncodedCommand is base64 of UTF-16LE text, not obfuscation
facts.fact: The -EncodedCommand parameter accepts a base64 string whose decoded bytes are UTF-16LE PowerShell source, which lets a caller avoid quoting problems when another program launches PowerShell. Because the encoding is trivial to reverse, it provides no confidentiality, and it is a common way to hide intent in logs that only record the process command line. Script block logging captures the decoded text when the engine compiles it, so detection should decode the argument and compare it with the logged script block rather than treating the flag itself as malicious.
details: The decoder is [Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetString([Convert]::FromBase64String($encoded)).
-EncodedCommand cannot be combined with -File or a command string in the same invocation.
Base64 of UTF-8 bytes decodes to mojibake because Windows PowerShell expects UTF-16LE.
The short form -e or -enc is equivalent and appears in process creation telemetry.
PowerShell 7 keeps the parameter for compatibility; the same decoding applies.
pitfalls: Treating any -EncodedCommand process as malicious; management tools use it legitimately.
Decoding with UTF-8 and concluding the payload is corrupt.

commands.purpose: Encode a short command the way -EncodedCommand expects it.
Decode an encoded command argument back to readable source for review.
Read recent script block logging events that contain the compiled script text.

mcqs.question: Which text encoding does -EncodedCommand expect before base64 encoding?
options: UTF-8
UTF-16LE
ASCII
UTF-32BE
mcqs.rationale: Windows PowerShell converts the command string with Encoding.Unicode, which is UTF-16LE on Windows. Passing base64 of UTF-8 bytes produces garbled source.

facts.title: SecureString protects memory, not storage or portability
facts.fact: A SecureString keeps the plaintext out of ordinary string variables and, on Windows, encrypts the buffer with DPAPI, but ConvertFrom-SecureString without -Key produces a blob bound to the user and machine that created it, so copying it to another host fails or requires the same key. A PSCredential bundles a user name with a SecureString for cmdlets that accept one. Persistent credentials belong in a secret store such as the SecretManagement extension with a vault, a managed identity, or a gMSA, never in a script literal or a repository file.
details: Get-Credential prompts interactively and returns a PSCredential; it does not persist anything.
ConvertFrom-SecureString -Key uses AES with a caller-supplied key, which moves the key management problem to you.
On Linux and macOS, PowerShell uses a different protection mechanism and SecureString is not equivalent to the Windows DPAPI path.
SecretManagement separates the secret store from the session: Register-SecretVault then Get-Secret.
Removing a secret from a variable does not erase copies in the process heap, crash dumps, or transcript files.
Transcripts and verbose logs can capture arguments, so avoid passing secrets on a command line.
pitfalls: Committing an exported SecureString blob because it looks encrypted.
Using -AsPlainText -Force in a script to build a credential from a literal password.

code.vulnerable:
$password = ConvertTo-SecureString 'not-a-real-password' -AsPlainText -Force
$cred = [pscredential]::new('svc-report', $password)
code.secure:
$secret = Get-Secret -Name 'svc-report' -Vault CorpVault
$cred = [pscredential]::new('svc-report', $secret)
code.issue: The first version embeds a plaintext secret in the script, where source control and logs can capture it. The second retrieves a SecureString from a registered vault, so the script contains no secret material.

misconceptions.claim: A SecureString is safe to store in a file because its contents are encrypted.
misconceptions.correction: ConvertFrom-SecureString without a key produces a DPAPI blob tied to the originating user and machine, and with a key the key must be protected too. Use a vault or platform identity; a SecureString protects in-memory handling, not at-rest storage.

facts.title: Invoke-Expression re-parses a string instead of binding parameters
facts.fact: Invoke-Expression takes a string and runs it as PowerShell source, which reintroduces parsing after the caller has already assembled the text, so a value containing a semicolon, pipe, or subexpression becomes new statements. The call operator & and the dot-source operator . invoke a command or script with arguments that are bound, not parsed, which is the correct replacement in almost every case. Where dynamic invocation is unavoidable, validate the command name against a fixed list and pass arguments through a hashtable or an array.
details: & $path @params splats a hashtable of named parameters without building source text.
Script block logging (event 4104) records the text that Invoke-Expression compiles, which is often the only evidence of the injected payload.
Module logging (event 4103) records pipeline execution for modules that enable it.
Transcription captures console input and output to a file, but it is not a substitute for script block logging.
AMSI can inspect the content that PowerShell submits for scanning, including decoded script.
pitfalls: Building a command string because the argument count is dynamic, instead of splatting an array or hashtable.
Believing that single-quoting the interpolated value makes Invoke-Expression safe.

code.vulnerable:
param([string]$Name)
Invoke-Expression "Get-Report -Name $Name"
code.secure:
param([string]$Name)
& (Join-Path $PSScriptRoot 'Get-Report.ps1') -Name $Name
code.issue: The first version concatenates input into PowerShell source, so the value can close the argument and add statements. The second binds the value as a parameter to a known script.

mcqs.question: What is the correct replacement for Invoke-Expression when calling a script with a user-supplied value?
options: Invoke-Command with -ScriptBlock { $value }
The call operator & with the script path and a named parameter
Start-Process with -ArgumentList as one string
Add-Type with the value as source
mcqs.rationale: & invokes the target and binds the value as an argument, so no second parse occurs. Start-Process with a single argument string can still be re-parsed by the target, and the other options execute or compile code.

facts.title: Windows PowerShell TLS defaults depend on the runtime, so pin the floor
facts.fact: Windows PowerShell 5.1 uses .NET Framework's ServicePointManager defaults, which vary with the installed framework and operating system and historically allowed TLS 1.0. Scripts that talk to modern endpoints often set [Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol explicitly, and the safe value is Tls12 or Tls13 rather than the legacy Tls or Ssl3 enumerations. PowerShell 7 uses .NET's HttpClient defaults instead, so ServicePointManager no longer controls those calls, and the newer -SkipCertificateCheck switch should be treated as a debugging aid only.
details: Setting SecurityProtocol to Tls12 replaces the list; use -bor to combine Tls12 and Tls13 where both are supported.
Certificate validation failures should be fixed at the trust store, not bypassed with a callback that returns true.
-SkipCertificateCheck exists on Invoke-RestMethod and Invoke-WebRequest in PowerShell 7 and later.
In PowerShell 7, configure handlers through HttpClientHandler or the -Certificate parameters rather than ServicePointManager.
TLS inspection proxies require their issuing CA in the trust store; disabling validation hides real interception.
pitfalls: Copying an old script that sets SecurityProtocol to Tls (1.0) and leaving it in place.
Bypassing certificate validation with a custom callback to silence an error in production.

code.vulnerable:
[Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol = [Net.SecurityProtocolType]::Tls
Invoke-RestMethod -Uri 'https://api.example.internal/health'
code.secure:
[Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol = [Net.SecurityProtocolType]::Tls12
Invoke-RestMethod -Uri 'https://api.example.internal/health'
code.issue: The first script pins TLS 1.0, which is deprecated and may be refused or downgraded. The second sets a modern floor for the Windows PowerShell call path.

references.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) best practices with .NET Framework

facts.title: SQL injection happens when data changes the parse tree
facts.fact: A statement is parsed into a syntax tree before execution, and values that are concatenated into the text become part of that tree; a single quote can end a string literal and the following characters are then read as SQL. The classic consequence is a WHERE clause that is always true, but the same mechanism supports UNION-based reads, stacked statements where the driver allows them, and calls to dangerous functions. Parameterisation is the primary fix because it binds values after parsing; escaping and blocklists only patch individual syntaxes and miss numeric contexts, comments, and vendor-specific quoting.
details: String concatenation in application code, dynamic SQL inside procedures, and ORM raw fragments all reach the same parser.
Numeric contexts need no quote at all, so quote-escaping filters do not protect them.
Least privilege limits what a successful injection can read or change, but does not prevent the injection.
A WAF is a compensating control at best; it cannot know the application's intended query shape.
Error messages that echo the statement or the DBMS version help an attacker refine the payload.
pitfalls: Replacing single quotes with two quotes and calling the query safe.
Assuming an ORM eliminates injection while still interpolating into raw SQL fragments.

code.issue: The concatenated version lets a quote in @email terminate the literal and add SQL. sp_executesql parses the statement with a parameter slot and binds @email as a value.

mcqs.question: Why does doubling single quotes fail to protect a numeric comparison such as WHERE id = <input>?
options: Numeric literals cannot contain quotes, so the escaping never runs
The database ignores doubled quotes in numeric context
Numeric context requires no quote to break out, so the input is already syntax
Doubling quotes only works in MySQL
mcqs.rationale: In a numeric position the attacker does not need to close a string; digits, spaces, and operators are already meaningful. This is why parameter binding, which is context independent, is preferred over escaping.

facts.title: Placeholders bind values; identifiers need an allowlist
facts.fact: A prepared statement separates parsing from execution: the server compiles a plan with parameter slots, then each execution supplies values that cannot alter the plan's structure. This is why placeholders work for literals in any position but cannot stand in for a table name, column name, sort direction, or keyword, because those choices change the parse tree. Dynamic identifiers should be mapped through a fixed allowlist to a known-safe token, and quoted with the platform function (QUOTENAME in SQL Server, quote_ident in PostgreSQL) as a second layer rather than as the primary check.
details: Prepared statements can be server-side or client-side; either way the value never becomes statement text.
Plan reuse is a performance benefit, but a generic plan can be slower for skewed data; that is a tuning decision, not a security one.
PostgreSQL EXECUTE ... USING passes values to a dynamic statement without concatenation.
SQL Server sp_executesql takes a parameter declaration string and a matching argument list.
Column allowlists should be small, literal, and reviewed; a map from user input to fixed SQL fragments is easy to audit.
pitfalls: Trying to bind an ORDER BY direction and falling back to concatenation when the driver rejects it.
Using quote_ident on unvalidated input and assuming quoting makes any identifier safe.

code.issue: Identifiers cannot be bound as parameters, but concatenating them lets input alter the statement. The secure form restricts both tokens to a fixed set and quotes the column before building the statement.

mcqs.question: Which part of a query can a bound parameter replace?
options: A table name in FROM
A column name in ORDER BY
A string or numeric literal compared in WHERE
The ASC or DESC keyword
mcqs.rationale: Parameters occupy value slots in an already parsed statement. Identifiers and keywords determine the shape of the parse tree and must come from an allowlist.

facts.title: The application account should not be able to change its own schema
facts.fact: An application needs DML on the tables it uses, not ownership of the database, and definitely not a server-wide administrative role. Separate accounts for migrations, reporting, and the runtime remove the ability to create objects, drop tables, or read unrelated schemas if the application is compromised. Grant only the verbs actually used (often SELECT, INSERT, and UPDATE, rarely DELETE), revoke default PUBLIC privileges on new schemas, and review role membership whenever a deployment adds a feature.
details: In PostgreSQL, CREATE on the public schema is granted to PUBLIC in older versions; revoke it and grant USAGE explicitly.
SQL Server's db_owner and sysadmin imply control over data and code, including the ability to impersonate or alter procedures.
A read-only reporting role that can read every schema still exposes data outside the report's purpose.
Ownership chaining lets a procedure access objects the caller cannot, which is useful but must be reviewed.
Rotate application credentials independently of migration credentials so a leak has a bounded blast radius.
Audit role membership and default roles after upgrades, because new default grants appear over time.
pitfalls: Granting db_owner to the application because an ORM migration needed it once.
Assuming a read-only account cannot be abused when it can read credentials or personal data.

commands.purpose: Create a runtime role with only the schema usage and table verbs the application needs.
Review exactly which table privileges the runtime role holds.

misconceptions.claim: A read-only database account is harmless if it is compromised.
misconceptions.correction: Read access is still data access: personal data, tokens, and internal configuration can be exfiltrated. Scope reads to the required tables and columns, and do not let the account reach schemas used by other services.

facts.title: Stored procedures inherit privilege, so dynamic SQL inside them is high impact
facts.fact: A procedure that runs with EXECUTE AS OWNER or relies on ownership chaining executes with rights the caller may not have, which is exactly why a dynamic statement built from a parameter inside it is more dangerous than the same concatenation in application code. In PostgreSQL, a SECURITY DEFINER function that resolves unqualified names through the caller's search_path can be tricked into using a different object. Keep procedure bodies parameterised, schema-qualify every object, avoid EXEC of assembled text, and grant EXECUTE only to the roles that need the procedure rather than direct table access.
details: EXECUTE AS OWNER is a deliberate privilege elevation; document why it is needed and what it can reach.
Ownership chaining applies when the procedure and the table share an owner, and it skips permission checks on the table.
In PostgreSQL, set a fixed search_path on SECURITY DEFINER functions to prevent object substitution.
SQL Server procedures can be signed with a certificate to grant narrow rights without ownership chaining.
Dynamic SQL inside a procedure should use sp_executesql with parameters, never EXEC(@string).
Review procedure ownership after restores and migrations, because owner changes alter the effective rights.
pitfalls: Assuming that because callers lack table permissions, a dynamic query inside the procedure is contained.
Leaving a SECURITY DEFINER function with the default search_path in PostgreSQL.

code.secure:
CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.run_report @actor nvarchar(100)
AS
BEGIN
    SELECT event_time, actor, action
    FROM dbo.audit_log
    WHERE actor = @actor;
END;
code.issue: The first procedure combines owner rights with a caller-supplied SQL fragment, so injection runs as the owner. The second removes the elevation and binds the value as a parameter to a fixed query.

mcqs.question: Why is SQL injection inside an EXECUTE AS OWNER procedure especially serious?
options: The procedure caches the injected statement for other users
The injected statement runs with the procedure owner's permissions rather than the caller's
EXECUTE AS disables parameter binding for the session
The procedure bypasses transaction logging
mcqs.rationale: The execution context is switched to the owner for the duration of the procedure, so an injected statement can reach objects the caller could not otherwise access.

facts.title: Row-level security only helps when the owner and bypass roles are handled
facts.fact: PostgreSQL row-level security attaches policies to a table and rewrites queries so rows failing the USING expression are invisible, with WITH CHECK enforcing the same rule on writes. Policies are combined per command, and permissive policies are ORed, so an extra policy can widen access unexpectedly. Two default behaviours surprise teams: the table owner bypasses RLS unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set, and roles with BYPASSRLS or superuser status ignore it entirely. Tenant context passed through a session setting must also be reset by the connection pool between borrowers.
details: Enable RLS with ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, then add at least one policy; without a policy the default is deny for non-owners.
FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY makes the owner subject to policies as well.
current_setting('app.tenant_id', true) returns NULL instead of raising when the setting is absent, which can fail closed or open depending on the policy.
A policy with USING (true) is permissive and combines with others via OR.
Connection poolers reuse sessions, so a tenant identifier set for one request can leak into the next unless it is cleared.
RLS does not protect against a role that can read the table's files or run as superuser.
pitfalls: Enabling RLS on a table owned by the application role and assuming the owner is filtered.
Testing only with the owner account, which bypasses every policy.

code.vulnerable:
ALTER TABLE invoices DISABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
GRANT SELECT ON invoices TO app_rw;
code.issue: Without RLS, every granted query sees every tenant's rows. The secure form filters rows by the session tenant for reads and writes and forces the owner through the same policy.

mcqs.question: A table has RLS enabled and a policy, but the application role owns the table and queries still return all rows. What is the most likely cause?
options: The policy needs a WITH CHECK clause to affect SELECT
The table owner bypasses RLS unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set
RLS only applies to UPDATE and DELETE
The role needs BYPASSRLS to see its own rows
mcqs.rationale: By default the owner is exempt from its own policies. FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY removes that exemption. WITH CHECK governs writes, not the read filter.

misconceptions.claim: Enabling row-level security is enough to isolate tenants.
misconceptions.correction: Policies must exist, the owner must be forced through them, and no application role may hold BYPASSRLS or superuser. Session tenant settings also have to be reset in pooled connections, or one request inherits another tenant's context.

facts.title: Blind injection extracts data one bit at a time from observable behaviour
facts.fact: When a query's output is not returned to the attacker, injection can still be exploited by asking the database yes/no questions and observing a difference: whether a page changes, whether a response is delayed, or whether an error occurs. Boolean-based inference encodes a condition into the result set, time-based inference uses conditional delays, and error-based inference forces a conversion or division error whose message reveals a value. The defence is the same parameterisation, but detection benefits from generic error pages, query timeouts, rate limiting, and least privilege, because each of those raises the cost of the oracle.
details: A single quote that produces a generic 500 response is already an oracle; consistent error handling removes the signal.
Time-based inference is noisy but can be amplified with repeated requests, so latency anomalies are worth alerting on.
Error-based techniques depend on verbose messages or on functions that embed data in an error, which is why production errors should not include statement text.
Parameterisation prevents the injected condition from existing, so no oracle remains.
Least privilege bounds what can be inferred even when an oracle exists.
pitfalls: Assuming that an endpoint which returns no query results is not injectable.
Relying on a WAF signature for boolean or time-based payloads rather than fixing the query.

mcqs.question: Which observation is the basis of time-based blind SQL injection?
options: The number of rows returned by the original query
A measurable delay that occurs only when an injected condition is true
The HTTP status code of the database health check
The length of the session cookie
mcqs.rationale: The attacker encodes a condition so that a true result triggers a delay (for example a conditional sleep) and a false result does not, turning response time into a one-bit channel.

misconceptions.claim: If the page never displays query results, SQL injection cannot be exploited.
misconceptions.correction: Blind techniques use side channels: different content, different status, different timing, or different errors. Removing output does not remove the injection, and it does not remove the oracle.

facts.title: Recursive merges of parsed JSON can write onto Object.prototype
facts.fact: JSON.parse creates an own property named __proto__ rather than changing the prototype, but a merge helper that recursively assigns target[key] = target[key] || {} then walks into target['__proto__'] reaches Object.prototype and writes attacker-chosen properties onto every object in the process. Depending on the framework, polluted keys such as isAdmin, shell, or env can change authorisation decisions or options passed to a child process. Defend by skipping __proto__, constructor, and prototype keys, using null-prototype dictionaries or Map for untrusted key sets, and validating the payload against a schema before merging.
details: Object.hasOwn(target, key) distinguishes an own property from one inherited through the prototype chain.
Object.freeze(Object.prototype) narrows the window but is not a complete defence and can break libraries.
Libraries that merge query strings, headers, or configuration objects are the usual entry points.
A Map has no prototype chain for string keys and is a better fit for arbitrary user-supplied key names.
Pollution is process-wide in Node.js, so one request can change behaviour for later requests.
Denial of service is also possible by replacing methods that later code calls.
pitfalls: Blocking only the literal string __proto__ while allowing constructor.prototype.
Assuming JSON.parse is safe because it does not evaluate code; the danger is in what the application does with the object.

code.issue: The recursive assignment follows the __proto__ accessor and writes onto Object.prototype. The secure version iterates own entries only, rejects the three dangerous keys, and builds results on null-prototype objects.

mcqs.question: Why does JSON.parse('{"__proto__": {"x": 1}}') not pollute by itself in Node.js?
options: JSON.parse rejects the __proto__ key
It creates an own data property named __proto__ instead of invoking the setter
The key is silently dropped by the parser
Prototype pollution only works in browsers
mcqs.rationale: The parser defines own properties and does not run the __proto__ setter. Pollution occurs when application code copies or merges that own property onto another object in a way that triggers the setter or reaches Object.prototype.

misconceptions.claim: JSON.parse is safe, so any object that came from JSON can be merged without checks.
misconceptions.correction: The parser is not the vulnerability; the merge is. A parsed document can carry __proto__ or constructor keys that a naive recursive assignment turns into prototype writes.

facts.title: HTML sinks parse strings as markup; text sinks do not
facts.fact: Assigning to innerHTML, outerHTML, insertAdjacentHTML, or document.write hands a string to the HTML parser, which builds elements and runs event handlers or javascript: URLs contained in it. textContent and createElement plus append set text nodes and attributes without parsing markup, so a value that contains < or & stays literal. When rich HTML is genuinely required, sanitise it with a maintained allowlist library such as DOMPurify and keep the sanitised fragment out of other interpreters; context matters, because a value safe in HTML text is not safe inside a script, style, or URL attribute.
details: element.setAttribute('href', value) still allows javascript: URLs; validate the scheme as well as escaping.
Template engines that autoescape HTML are not automatically safe in attribute or JavaScript contexts.
Trusted Types in Chromium turns DOM sink assignments into a checked boundary that requires a policy.
Server-side sanitisation helps, but client-side rendering must also avoid parsing untrusted strings.
A Content Security Policy that blocks inline script reduces impact but does not fix the sink.
Event handler attributes and <iframe srcdoc> are HTML sinks that are easy to overlook.
pitfalls: Escaping < and > by hand and missing quotes, ampersands, or URL contexts.
Using innerHTML with an empty string to clear a node when replaceChildren() is clearer and safer.

code.issue: innerHTML parses the query value as markup, so an injected element or handler executes. textContent creates a text node and renders the same characters literally.

mcqs.question: Which assignment avoids executing markup supplied in a URL parameter?
options: element.innerHTML = value
element.insertAdjacentHTML('beforeend', value)
element.textContent = value
document.write(value)
mcqs.rationale: Only textContent treats the value as text. The other three invoke the HTML parser, which can create elements and event handlers from the string.

facts.title: eval, new Function, and string timers all compile code at runtime
facts.fact: eval runs a string in the caller's scope, new Function compiles a string into a function in global scope, and setTimeout or setInterval with a string argument evaluates it; all three turn data into executable code and defeat CSP unless unsafe-eval is allowed. They also break static analysis, minification assumptions, and source maps. Data should be parsed with JSON.parse, and behaviour selected from a fixed table of functions or a small interpreter rather than assembled from strings.
details: eval in strict mode still executes code; strict mode only changes the scope rules.
Indirect eval, (0, eval)(code), runs in global scope and is not safer.
A CSP with script-src without unsafe-eval blocks eval and new Function, which is a useful backstop.
setTimeout accepts a function; passing a string is the legacy form and should be removed.
Node's vm module is not a security boundary for untrusted code; use a separate process or isolate.
pitfalls: Sanitising the string before eval and believing the result is safe.
Using new Function to implement a calculation feature that could be a small parser.

code.issue: eval executes any expression supplied by the caller. The secure version looks the rule up in a fixed table, so input selects behaviour but never becomes source code.

mcqs.question: Which CSP directive most directly limits the impact of an eval-based sink?
options: default-src 'self'
script-src without 'unsafe-eval'
img-src 'none'
frame-ancestors 'none'
mcqs.rationale: Eval and new Function require the unsafe-eval source expression. Omitting it makes the browser block those compilations, which is a backstop rather than a substitute for removing the sink.

references.title: CWE-95: Improper Neutralization of Directives in Dynamically Evaluated Code

facts.title: JavaScript deserialisation gadgets hide in revivers and old libraries
facts.fact: Plain JSON is data, but code that revives it can execute functions: a JSON.parse reviver that assigns attacker keys onto prototypes pollutes the process, and legacy libraries such as node-serialize encoded functions in a marker property and eval'd them on deserialise. The risk grows when serialised state crosses a trust boundary, for example a cookie, a job queue payload, or a cached session. Prefer JSON with an explicit schema, never pass user data to a reviver that writes to shared objects, and treat any library that advertises function serialisation as unsafe for untrusted input.
details: A reviver runs for every key, including nested ones, so a single branch on a dangerous key can pollute globally.
Prototype pollution through a reviver is the same primitive as a merge bug, with the same impact.
Node's v8.deserialize and structuredClone are for trusted internal data, not for attacker-supplied bytes.
Schema validation libraries reject unknown keys, which also reduces gadget surface.
Signing serialised cookies prevents tampering but not a gadget chain if the signer is compromised.
pitfalls: Trusting a value because it is base64-encoded rather than encrypted.
Assuming a JSON content type means the parser was the only thing that touched the data.

code.issue: The reviver copies an attacker-controlled object onto Object.prototype. The secure parser accepts only known keys with known types and stores them on a null-prototype object.

facts.title: npm lifecycle scripts run automatically with the installing user's rights
facts.fact: npm runs preinstall, install, and postinstall scripts declared by a dependency during installation, so adding a package grants its author code execution on the developer machine and on CI, often with access to tokens and the repository. A lockfile plus npm ci makes the resolved tree reproducible, and --ignore-scripts suppresses lifecycle execution when the project does not need native builds. Dependency confusion exploits unscoped or misconfigured lookups by publishing a higher-version package with an internal name to a public registry, so scope internal names and point those scopes at an internal registry.
details: npm ci installs exactly the lockfile and fails if package.json and the lockfile disagree, which is preferable in CI.
The scripts run with the user's full environment, including registry tokens and cloud credentials.
Scope configuration in .npmrc maps @corp packages to a private registry and prevents public fallback.
Provenance attestations link a published package to a source repository and build, which raises the cost of impersonation.
Optional dependencies and transitive packages also run lifecycle scripts.
Review new direct dependencies and lockfile diffs rather than only auditing known CVEs.
pitfalls: Assuming a package is safe because it has no install script; a dependency of a dependency may have one.
Relying on npm audit alone, which does not detect malicious packages without advisories.

commands.purpose: Install exactly the lockfile without running dependency lifecycle scripts.
Confirm which registry the current configuration resolves packages from.
Check production dependencies against the advisory database.
Inspect the full dependency tree, including transitive packages.

configs.purpose: Route the internal scope to a private registry and keep the public registry for everything else.

mcqs.question: Which npm command installs the locked dependency tree without executing install lifecycle scripts?
options: npm install --production
npm ci --ignore-scripts
npm audit fix
npm update --no-save
mcqs.rationale: npm ci uses the lockfile for a reproducible install, and --ignore-scripts disables preinstall, install, and postinstall execution. npm install may rewrite the lockfile, and audit fix changes versions.

facts.title: Server-rendered HTML is an output context, not a trusted one
facts.fact: Server-side rendering builds a string that the browser parses as HTML, so any request-derived value placed into that string is subject to the same context rules as client-side code. A common mistake is serialising application state into an inline script with JSON.stringify, because a value containing </script> closes the element early and a U+2028 or U+2029 can break older parsers. Escape for the script context, or put the state in a JSON script type and parse it, and remember that React escapes children but dangerouslySetInnerHTML bypasses that protection.
details: HTML escaping is not sufficient inside a script element; the closing tag sequence must not appear in the text.
A <script type="application/json"> block read with JSON.parse avoids the inline executable context.
Template engines differ in autoescaping defaults and in which contexts they understand; verify the engine's escaping for attributes and scripts.
Hydration mismatches can indicate that the server and client rendered different, potentially unsafe, data.
Frameworks that stream HTML need the same escaping at every flush point, including error pages.
Do not embed secrets in serialised state; the client can read everything the server sends.
pitfalls: Escaping only &, <, and > for HTML text and reusing that output inside a script block.
Assuming a component framework escapes values passed to dangerouslySetInnerHTML.

code.issue: JSON.stringify does not escape <, so a string containing </script> terminates the block and the remainder is parsed as HTML. The secure serialiser escapes the HTML-significant characters and the JavaScript line separators.

mcqs.question: Why is JSON.stringify alone insufficient for state embedded in an inline script element?
options: JSON.stringify cannot serialise nested objects
It leaves < unescaped, so a value containing </script> closes the element
It converts numbers to strings
It always throws on Unicode input
mcqs.rationale: The HTML parser looks for the literal closing tag sequence before JavaScript ever runs. Escaping < as \u003c keeps the text inside the element while preserving the parsed value.

misconceptions.claim: A React application is not vulnerable to XSS because JSX escapes interpolated values.
misconceptions.correction: JSX escapes text children, but dangerouslySetInnerHTML, URLs assigned to href, and server-built HTML strings bypass that. Escaping is context specific, and the framework only covers the contexts it controls.

references.title: Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet

facts.title: html/template escapes per context; text/template escapes nothing
facts.fact: html/template parses a template, tracks whether each action sits in HTML text, an attribute, a URL, JavaScript, or CSS, and applies the escaping function for that context. text/template performs no escaping and is intended for plain text, logs, or code generation, so using it to build a web page turns every interpolated value into a potential cross-site scripting sink. Import html/template for anything a browser will parse, and reserve template.HTML for values that have already been sanitised by a trusted process.
details: Autoescaping applies to actions; a value injected into template source itself is not escaped.
template.HTML, template.JS, template.URL and similar types bypass escaping and should be treated as trusted assertions.
html/template also rewrites URL attributes and blocks javascript: schemes in some positions.
Templates that are parsed from user input are a different, much worse problem; templates are code.
Use template.Must only for templates fixed at build time, since it panics on parse errors.
pitfalls: Converting a value to template.HTML to make markup render, which reintroduces the sink.
Testing with benign input and concluding the escaping is correct for attributes and scripts.

code.issue: text/template writes the value verbatim, so markup in name becomes elements. html/template applies HTML-text escaping for this context.

mcqs.question: Which package should render a value into an HTML attribute in a web response?
options: text/template, because it preserves formatting
html/template, because it tracks the HTML context and escapes accordingly
fmt.Fprintf with %s
encoding/json
mcqs.rationale: html/template determines the context of each action and applies the matching escaper, including attribute and URL contexts. The other options either do no escaping or escape for a different grammar.

misconceptions.claim: html/template escapes every value, so template.HTML is just a formatting convenience.
misconceptions.correction: template.HTML tells the engine that the value is already safe, so it is inserted without escaping. It is a trust assertion; converting untrusted input to it disables the protection.

facts.title: filepath.Join cleans a path but does not confine it
facts.fact: filepath.Join calls Clean, which removes . and .. segments lexically, but cleaning does not keep the result under the base: filepath.Join("/srv/files", "../../etc/passwd") still resolves outside, and an absolute second element on some code paths discards the base. Confinement requires an explicit check, such as filepath.IsLocal on the relative name (Go 1.20) followed by a filepath.Rel comparison against the base, or os.Root (Go 1.24) for open operations that cannot escape even through symlinks. Keep filepath for operating-system paths and path for slash-separated URL or import paths; mixing them produces different traversal behaviour.
details: filepath.IsLocal reports whether a path is relative and stays within its directory, rejecting .. and absolute names.
os.Root scopes Open, Create, and related calls to a directory and rejects traversal and symlink escapes.
Percent-decoding happens before routing, so validate the decoded value, not the raw URL segment.
On Windows, volume names, drive-relative paths, and alternate data streams add escape forms that a POSIX mental model misses.
path.Clean works on slash-separated paths and is the right tool for URL path normalisation, not for disk access.
pitfalls: Assuming filepath.Clean makes a path safe, when it only normalises it.
Concatenating with a slash instead of using Join and then skipping validation because the code 'already joins'.

code.issue: Join normalises ../../ but leaves the result outside base. The secure version rejects non-local names and verifies the relative path back to the base before opening.

mcqs.question: What does filepath.Join(base, name) guarantee about name?
options: That the result is inside base
That the result is lexically cleaned, but not that it stays inside base
That name is percent-decoded
That symlinks are resolved
mcqs.rationale: Join cleans the concatenation. Traversal segments can still lead outside the base, and symlinks are not resolved, so an explicit containment check is required.

facts.title: math/rand is deterministic; tokens need crypto/rand
facts.fact: math/rand and math/rand/v2 implement fast pseudo-random generators intended for simulation, shuffling, and jitter, and their output is reproducible from a seed. They must not produce keys, session identifiers, password-reset tokens, or nonces. crypto/rand.Read fills a byte slice from the operating system CSPRNG and returns an error that must be handled; encoding the bytes with base64.RawURLEncoding gives a compact token without padding. In Go 1.24, crypto/rand.Text returns a random string intended for exactly this use.
details: math/rand's global source is seeded deterministically in older Go versions unless Seed is called; Go 1.20 seeds it randomly but that still does not make it cryptographic.
crypto/rand.Read never returns a short read without an error, but ignoring the error is still a bug.
For modulo-free selection from a small alphabet, use crypto/rand.Int with a big.Int bound or rejection sampling.
Nonces and salts have the same unpredictability requirement as keys.
Testing code can use math/rand; production secret generation cannot.
pitfalls: Seeding math/rand with the current time and calling the result unpredictable.
Using math/rand.Intn for a password generator and then base64-encoding the result.

code.issue: math/rand is predictable and unsuitable for secrets. crypto/rand reads from the OS CSPRNG and propagates failure instead of silently returning weak bytes.

mcqs.question: Which Go package should generate a password-reset token?
options: math/rand
math/rand/v2
crypto/rand
hash/fnv
mcqs.rationale: crypto/rand is the interface to the operating system CSPRNG. Both math/rand packages are deterministic PRNGs, and hash/fnv is a non-cryptographic hash.

facts.title: exec.Command does not use a shell unless you ask for one
facts.fact: exec.Command resolves the program with LookPath and passes each argument as a separate element of argv, so a value containing spaces, quotes, or semicolons is delivered as one argument and is not interpreted. Injection reappears when the program is sh or cmd with -c and a concatenated string, because then a shell parses the text. Use CommandContext for timeouts and cancellation, pass -- before user-controlled operands where the tool supports it, and set Env explicitly when the child must not inherit credentials.
details: LookPath searches PATH, so the program name itself is subject to PATH hijacking.
cmd.Env = append(os.Environ(), ...) inherits everything; start from a minimal slice when that matters.
CombinedOutput captures stdout and stderr but buffers everything in memory, which is a risk for large output.
On Windows, batch files are run through cmd.exe, which reintroduces shell parsing for .bat and .cmd targets.
