Set cmd.Stdin carefully; an interactive child can block forever without a timeout.
pitfalls: Switching to sh -c to get pipes or redirection and then interpolating a filename into the string.
Ignoring the error from Run and assuming the command succeeded.

code.issue: The first version asks a shell to parse a concatenated string, so name can add commands. The second passes name as a single argv element with no shell and adds a deadline.

facts.title: Set a TLS floor and never disable certificate verification
facts.fact: crypto/tls will negotiate older protocol versions unless MinVersion is raised, and InsecureSkipVerify removes hostname and chain validation entirely, turning the connection into unauthenticated encryption. A client should set MinVersion to tls.VersionTLS12 or higher, leave verification enabled, and rely on ServerName or the URL host for identity; a server should also choose a certificate, set MinVersion, and prefer the default cipher suites maintained by the standard library. Custom VerifyPeerCertificate callbacks must actually perform the verification they replace.
details: TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are deprecated by RFC 8996 and should not be negotiated.
InsecureSkipVerify is occasionally used with a custom verification callback, but the callback then carries the whole burden.
RootCAs replaces the system pool rather than adding to it; use x509.SystemCertPool and append.
Client certificates require both Certificates and a verification policy on the server side.
tls.Config values must not be modified after first use; clone a shared config before changing it.
Handshake timeouts belong on the listener or dialer, not only on the TLS config.
pitfalls: Copying InsecureSkipVerify: true from a test helper into production code.
Setting MinVersion but leaving MaxVersion at an old value that prevents TLS 1.3.

code.issue: InsecureSkipVerify accepts any certificate, so a network attacker can impersonate the server. The secure version keeps verification and sets a modern protocol floor.

mcqs.question: What is the effect of tls.Config{InsecureSkipVerify: true} on a client connection?
options: It disables encryption but keeps authentication
It disables certificate chain and hostname verification while still encrypting
It forces TLS 1.2 as the minimum version
It uses a self-signed certificate automatically
mcqs.rationale: The handshake still encrypts, but the client no longer proves the server's identity, so an active attacker can present any certificate and read or modify the traffic.

facts.title: go.sum and the checksum database detect changed module content
facts.fact: The go command records a cryptographic hash of every module it uses in go.sum and, by default, verifies new modules against the public checksum database sum.golang.org, which makes a silent rewrite of an existing version detectable even if the proxy is malicious. GOPRIVATE and GONOSUMDB-style patterns are for private modules that cannot be published to that database, and GONOSUMDB removes the transparency check for matching paths, so scope it narrowly. Commit go.sum for applications, run go mod verify when integrity is in question, and remember that a checksum proves the bytes match what was published, not that the code is safe.
details: The checksum database is append-only and transparent; a mismatch fails the build instead of warning.
GOFLAGS=-mod=readonly prevents a build from silently editing go.mod or go.sum in CI.
GONOSUMDB is the older spelling; GOPRIVATE sets both GONOPROXY and GONOSUMDB for matching module paths in current releases.
A private proxy can serve private modules, but its content should still be reviewed and pinned.
go mod verify checks the module cache against go.sum, not against the remote source.
Replacing a module with a local path bypasses checksum checks, which is fine for development and dangerous if it reaches a release build.
pitfalls: Deleting go.sum entries to resolve a mismatch instead of investigating why the content changed.
Setting GOPRIVATE=* and disabling the checksum database for every module.

commands.purpose: Check that the downloaded module cache still matches the hashes recorded in go.sum.
Inspect which checksum database and privacy patterns the toolchain will apply.
List the full module graph that the build will use.

misconceptions.claim: A matching go.sum entry proves the dependency is free of vulnerabilities.
misconceptions.correction: The checksum proves the downloaded bytes equal the bytes that were published for that version. It says nothing about whether those bytes are safe, so advisory scanning and review remain necessary.

facts.title: A uintptr is an integer, not a live reference
facts.fact: unsafe.Pointer conversions are governed by a small set of rules: a Pointer may be converted to uintptr only for immediate arithmetic in the same expression, because uintptr does not keep the object alive and the garbage collector may move or free it between statements. Storing the integer in a variable and converting it back later is therefore invalid even when it appears to work. Use unsafe.Add for pointer arithmetic and unsafe.Slice to build a slice from a pointer and length, keep the unsafe block as small as possible, and run tests with -race and the checkptr instrumentation to catch violations.
details: The valid pattern is p = unsafe.Pointer(uintptr(p) + offset) in one expression, and unsafe.Add expresses it more clearly.
unsafe.Slice(ptr, len) replaces the older reflect.SliceHeader construction, which was easy to get wrong.
checkptr runs under -race and -d=checkptr, reporting conversions that violate the rules.
unsafe.String and unsafe.StringData (Go 1.20) cover the string equivalents.
A Pointer must not point to Go memory after that memory is no longer reachable by any typed pointer.
Violations are undefined behaviour, not guaranteed crashes, so the absence of a failure is not evidence of correctness.
pitfalls: Caching a uintptr in a struct field to avoid keeping a reference alive.
Assuming that because the collector is non-moving today, uintptr round-trips are portable across future versions.

code.issue: The first version stores a uintptr, which does not keep the slice alive, and then converts it back in a later statement; it also reads past the end for short slices. unsafe.Add keeps the pointer typed, and the length check prevents the out-of-bounds access.

facts.title: unsafe disables the compiler's proof obligations, not the rules
facts.fact: An unsafe block does not turn off bounds checks or the borrow checker inside it; it grants the programmer permission to perform operations the compiler cannot verify, such as dereferencing a raw pointer or calling an unsafe function. The code must still satisfy Rust's invariants: references must be aligned, non-null, and valid for their lifetime; a &mut must be unique and a & must not alias a mutation; values must be initialised and valid for their type. Each block should be as small as possible, carry a comment stating why the invariants hold, and be tested with Miri when the code performs raw pointer or layout tricks.
details: Creating two &mut references to the same element is undefined behaviour even if neither is written through.
transmute requires identical size and compatible validity; prefer From, TryFrom, or a union for conversions.
Miri interprets the code and detects many aliasing and validity violations that ordinary tests miss.
A safe wrapper around unsafe code must not expose an API that lets safe callers break the invariants.
Pointers derived from a reference are subject to provenance rules; do not manufacture them from integers.
Uninitialised memory, padding bytes, and bools with values other than 0 or 1 are invalid even when only read.
pitfalls: Assuming that if the code compiles and the tests pass, the unsafe block is sound.
Wrapping a large function in unsafe instead of isolating the one operation that needs it.

code.issue: The first function hands out two mutable references to the same element, which violates uniqueness. split_first_mut produces disjoint borrows that the compiler can verify.

mcqs.question: What does an unsafe block actually change?
options: It disables bounds checks for the whole module
It allows operations the compiler cannot verify, while the programmer must uphold the invariants
It turns off the borrow checker inside the block
It makes panics abort instead of unwind
mcqs.rationale: unsafe is an assertion by the programmer that the listed operations meet Rust's rules. Bounds checks and type checking still apply, and violating the invariants is undefined behaviour.

references.title: The Rust Programming Language - Unsafe Rust
The Rustonomicon - Meet Safe and Unsafe

facts.title: Release builds wrap on overflow unless checks are enabled
facts.fact: Arithmetic on unsigned integers wraps in release builds, while debug builds panic, so a size calculation can abort in development and silently produce a small value in production. A release profile can enable overflow-checks, and the standard library offers checked_*, saturating_*, overflowing_*, and wrapping_* methods to make the intent explicit. Security-sensitive size and offset computations should use checked arithmetic and propagate None or an error, because a wrapped allocation size followed by a larger copy is a classic heap overflow.
details: profile.release.overflow-checks = true restores panics in release builds at a performance cost.
as casts truncate silently in every profile; use TryFrom for narrowing conversions.
usize is pointer-sized, so a calculation that fits on 64-bit may wrap on a 32-bit target.
In debug builds the panic message names the operation and the operands, which helps locate the bug.
Vec::with_capacity can abort the process on an impossible capacity, which is a denial of service rather than corruption.
pitfalls: Testing only with debug builds and never exercising the release profile.
Believing that release mode is safe because it does not panic on overflow.

code.issue: The unchecked multiplication wraps in release builds, so a huge dimension yields a small allocation that a later copy overruns. checked_mul returns None instead of wrapping.

mcqs.question: What happens to an overflowing usize multiplication in a default release build?
options: It panics with an overflow message
It saturates at usize::MAX
It wraps modulo 2^usize::BITS
It returns an error through the Result type
mcqs.rationale: Overflow checks are enabled in debug builds and disabled by default in release. Without checks the operation wraps, which is why size arithmetic should use checked_mul or an explicit wrapping method.

facts.title: A panic is not an error channel, and unwinding across FFI is fatal
facts.fact: By default a panic unwinds, running destructors until it reaches a catch_unwind boundary or the thread root; panic = abort skips unwinding entirely. Unwinding out of an extern "C" function is undefined behaviour in older editions and aborts since Rust 1.81, so an FFI callback must catch panics before returning. catch_unwind only catches unwinding panics, requires UnwindSafe (or an explicit assertion), and should not be used to implement ordinary error handling because it cannot report why the failure happened. A panic that occurs while a Mutex is held poisons the mutex, which later lockers must handle explicitly.
details: AssertUnwindSafe is a promise that the captured state is still consistent after a panic; it is not a check.
panic = abort in the release profile removes landing pads but also removes the ability to catch.
Library code should generally return Result for expected failures and reserve panic for bugs.
A panic in a destructor during unwinding aborts the process.
tokio tasks catch panics at the task boundary, so a panicking task does not take down the runtime.
Cross-language callbacks need a defined error return, not a propagated panic.
pitfalls: Using catch_unwind as a try/catch substitute and losing the panic message.
Letting a panic cross an extern "C" boundary and assuming the caller will handle it.

code.issue: The first function lets a panic unwind across the C ABI, which aborts or is undefined depending on the compiler version. The secure version catches the panic inside the callback and returns an error code.

mcqs.question: Why must a Rust function exported with extern "C" not unwind into its caller?
options: The C caller cannot represent a Rust Result type
Unwinding across the C ABI has no defined behaviour and aborts on current compilers
It disables destructors for the whole process
It converts the panic into a segmentation fault
mcqs.rationale: The C ABI has no unwinding contract, so a panic crossing the boundary is not something the caller can handle. Current Rust aborts at the boundary; catching inside the callback is the supported pattern.

facts.title: A plain zeroing loop can be optimised away; zeroize uses volatile writes
facts.fact: Writing zeros over a buffer that is never read again is a dead store, and the optimiser is allowed to remove it, so a hand-written wipe may leave the secret in memory. The zeroize crate uses volatile writes and a compiler fence, and implements Zeroize for common containers so the wipe happens before the allocation is released. Constant-time comparison is a separate concern: subtle's ConstantTimeEq compares without early exit, while ordinary slice equality can return at the first differing byte. Neither crate can erase copies made by the operating system, a debugger, or a swap file.
details: SecretString and SecretBox from secrecy wrap values, zeroize on drop, and avoid Debug output.
Deriving Debug or Clone on a struct that holds key material creates extra copies and log exposure.
zeroize(drop) clears the original allocation, but a reallocation may have left an older copy behind.
subtle::ConstantTimeEq returns a Choice that must be converted with into() or unwrap_u8().
Large secrets are better kept in memory locked against swapping, which is platform specific and outside std.
Do not rely on zeroization as the only control; minimise lifetime and exposure first.
pitfalls: Using memset through FFI and assuming the call cannot be elided because it is a function call.
Comparing MACs or tokens with == on byte slices and treating the timing difference as theoretical.

code.issue: The compiler may delete the plain writes because the buffer is not read afterwards. Zeroize performs volatile writes with a fence so the wipe is observable.

mcqs.question: Why is a hand-written loop that sets each byte to zero not a reliable secret wipe?
options: Rust forbids writing to borrowed buffers
The optimiser may remove the writes as dead stores
Zero bytes are invalid for u8
It only clears the first cache line
mcqs.rationale: Without volatile semantics and a compiler barrier, the writes have no observable effect and can be eliminated. The zeroize crate exists to make the wipe survive optimisation.

misconceptions.claim: Calling memset on a key buffer guarantees the key is erased from memory.
misconceptions.correction: A normal memset can be optimised away when the buffer is dead, and it cannot reach copies in registers, other allocations, core dumps, or swap. Use a zeroizing type, keep the secret lifetime short, and treat memory clearing as best effort.

facts.title: std::process::Command passes arguments directly, without a shell
facts.fact: Command::new(program).arg(a).arg(b) resolves the program and passes each argument as a separate element of argv, so spaces and metacharacters inside an argument are not interpreted. Injection requires an explicit shell, such as Command::new("sh").arg("-c").arg(concatenated), and that pattern should be avoided for untrusted values. Use -- before operands where the tool supports it, set env_clear or a minimal environment when the child must not inherit credentials, and prefer status() or output() over spawn() so the exit status is checked.
details: The program name itself is resolved through PATH unless it contains a slash, so it is also a lookup decision.
Windows batch files are executed through cmd.exe, which reintroduces parsing for .bat and .cmd targets.
output() captures stdout and stderr but waits for the child, so a hung child needs an external timeout.
std::process has no built-in timeout; use wait_timeout or a supervising thread for untrusted children.
arg("--") is only meaningful if the target program implements the end-of-options convention.
Inherited environment variables can include tokens; env_clear plus explicit variables is the narrow option.
pitfalls: Reaching for sh -c to get a pipeline and interpolating a filename into the command string.
Using spawn() and never calling wait, leaving a zombie and losing the exit status.

code.issue: The first version hands a formatted string to a shell, so name can add commands or options. The second passes fixed arguments to tar with an end-of-options marker and no shell.

mcqs.question: Which Rust call reintroduces shell parsing for user-controlled data?
options: Command::new("tar").arg("-czf").arg(path)
Command::new("sh").arg("-c").arg(format!("tar -czf {path}"))
Command::new("tar").args(["-czf", path])
Command::new("/usr/bin/tar").arg(path)
mcqs.rationale: Only the sh -c form puts a shell between the program and the data. The other forms pass each argument as a separate argv element.

facts.title: cargo-audit checks the lockfile against RustSec advisories
facts.fact: cargo-audit reads Cargo.lock, matches the resolved crate versions against the RustSec advisory database, and reports vulnerable, unmaintained, and yanked dependencies. It audits what is locked, so binaries should commit Cargo.lock and CI should run the audit against that file. cargo-deny adds policy checks for licenses, duplicate versions, and untrusted registries, while cargo tree -d shows multiple versions of the same crate, which often signals an unmaintained transitive dependency. None of these tools detect a malicious crate with no advisory, so review new dependencies as well.
details: RustSec advisories carry an ID, affected version ranges, and often a patched version.
cargo audit --deny warnings turns findings into a non-zero exit status in CI.
The advisory database can be updated locally with cargo audit fetch.
Libraries usually do not commit Cargo.lock, but applications and services should.
cargo deny check advisories can replace cargo audit in a policy-driven pipeline.
A yanked crate is not necessarily vulnerable, but it should not be added to a new build.
pitfalls: Auditing a workspace without a lockfile, so the tool sees only the manifest ranges.
Assuming a clean advisory scan means the dependency is trustworthy.

commands.purpose: Match Cargo.lock against RustSec advisories and list vulnerable dependencies.

commands.code: cargo deny check advisories bans licenses sources
commands.purpose: Apply advisory, duplicate, license, and registry policy in one CI step.
Show crates that are resolved at more than one version.

misconceptions.claim: cargo-audit protects against malicious crates published to crates.io.
misconceptions.correction: The tool compares versions against known advisories. A newly published malicious crate has no advisory, so dependency review, minimal dependency sets, and build provenance remain necessary.

facts.title: Rust TLS stacks verify by default; disabling verification is explicit
facts.fact: rustls verifies the server certificate chain and hostname by default, supports only TLS 1.2 and 1.3, and does not read the operating system trust store unless the application loads it through rustls-native-certs or webpki-roots. Client builders in higher-level crates expose danger_accept_invalid_certs and danger_accept_invalid_hostnames, both of which must be treated as test-only switches. Alpn protocols, SNI, and root certificates are configuration decisions that affect security, and a custom certificate verifier replaces the whole validation policy rather than adding to it.
details: rustls rejects IP-address certificates unless the target is configured correctly; SNI is not sent for IPs.
The default crypto provider must be selected explicitly in rustls 0.23 (ring or aws-lc-rs).
Adding a private CA means extending the root store, not disabling verification.
Certificate pinning can be layered on top with a custom verifier, but it must still perform normal validation first.
A self-signed certificate in production is a trust decision that every client must ship.
TLS termination at a proxy moves the verification requirement to the proxy configuration.
pitfalls: Using danger_accept_invalid_certs to work around a missing private CA.
Assuming rustls uses the system trust store automatically and shipping a client that trusts nothing.

code.issue: The first client accepts any certificate, so an active attacker can impersonate the server. The second keeps verification and sets an explicit protocol floor.

facts.title: Unbounded string functions write past the end of the destination
facts.fact: strcpy, strcat, and sprintf copy until they reach a terminator in the source, with no knowledge of the destination's size, so a longer input overwrites whatever follows the buffer on the stack or heap. Bounded replacements still have traps: strncpy does not terminate when the source is at least as long as the limit and pads the rest of the destination with zeros, while snprintf returns the length the output would have needed, so the return value must be compared with the buffer size before the result is used. Prefer snprintf, check its return value, and size every destination from the same constant used in the copy.
details: The off-by-one form is easy to miss: snprintf(buf, sizeof buf, ...) is correct, snprintf(buf, sizeof buf - 1, ...) needlessly truncates.
strlcpy and strlcat are available on BSD-derived systems and some libc implementations but are not portable C.
memcpy with a length derived from untrusted input is the same bug when the destination is smaller.
A missing terminator turns a later strlen or %s into an out-of-bounds read.
FORTIFY_SOURCE can catch some cases at runtime when the compiler knows the object size and optimisation is enabled.
Compiler warnings such as -Wformat-overflow and -Wstringop-truncation flag many of these patterns before runtime.
pitfalls: Assuming strncpy always null-terminates because the size argument is present.
Checking snprintf's return value only for negative values and ignoring truncation.

code.issue: strcpy and strcat do not know the destination size, so a long name overflows message. snprintf bounds the write and its return value detects truncation.

mcqs.question: What does strncpy(dst, src, n) guarantee when strlen(src) >= n?
options: dst is null-terminated at dst[n-1]
No terminator is written, so dst may not be a valid C string
The function returns an error
The remaining bytes of dst are left unchanged
mcqs.rationale: strncpy copies at most n bytes and only pads with zeros when the source is shorter. When the source fills the limit, the destination has no terminator, and later string operations read past it.

misconceptions.claim: strncpy is the safe version of strcpy, so using it removes the overflow risk.
misconceptions.correction: strncpy bounds the copy but can leave the destination unterminated, and it zero-fills the remainder, which is costly for large buffers. It prevents the write overflow only when n is the destination size and you terminate explicitly.

references.title: CWE-120: Buffer Copy without Checking Size of Input

facts.title: An off-by-one and an integer overflow often combine into heap corruption
facts.fact: A loop written as i <= count over an array of count elements writes one element past the end, and a size computed as rows * width in int arithmetic can overflow before it reaches malloc, producing a small allocation followed by a large copy. Both defects are silent in the sense that the allocation succeeds and the copy runs; damage appears later when heap metadata or an adjacent object is used. Compute sizes in size_t with an explicit overflow check, use the same bound for allocation and iteration, and test with AddressSanitizer, which places red zones around allocations and reports the first invalid access.
details: Signed overflow in C is undefined behaviour, so the compiler may assume it cannot happen and optimise the check away.
rows * width can overflow even when each value is small, because int is often 32 bits.
Use calloc(count, size) to get the multiplication checked by the allocator, and prefer it for arrays.
Loop conditions should use i < count for zero-based indexing; <= is correct only for inclusive bounds.
AddressSanitizer detects the write at the moment it happens, which is far easier to diagnose than a later crash.
UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer catches the signed overflow that precedes the heap overflow.
pitfalls: Checking for overflow after the multiplication has already been performed.
Fixing the loop bound but leaving the allocation size calculation unchanged.

code.issue: The signed multiplication can overflow before the cast, and the <= loop writes one byte past the allocation. The secure version checks the multiplication in size_t and removes the out-of-bounds loop.

mcqs.question: Why is checking rows * width > SIZE_MAX / width after computing the product ineffective?
options: SIZE_MAX is not available for size_t
The multiplication has already overflowed, so the check sees a wrapped value
The compiler always removes the comparison
Division is slower than multiplication
mcqs.rationale: The guard must be evaluated before the product, for example rows > SIZE_MAX / width. Once the multiplication has wrapped, the comparison operates on a meaningless value.

facts.title: Passing input as the format string lets it read and write memory
facts.fact: printf treats its first argument as a format specification, so a caller-controlled string containing %x, %s, or %n causes the function to consume arguments that were never supplied and to interpret them as pointers. %n writes the number of characters printed so far through a pointer taken from the argument list, which is a write primitive, while %s reads from an arbitrary address and can crash or leak. The format string must always be a fixed literal, with input passed as a corresponding argument: printf("%s", input).
details: The same rule applies to fprintf, sprintf, snprintf, syslog, and any function with a printf-style signature.
Compilers warn about non-literal format strings with -Wformat-security and -Wformat-nonliteral.
A literal that contains no conversions and no arguments is safe: fputs(input, stdout) is equivalent and clearer.
Width and precision specifiers in attacker input can also cause large reads or output amplification.
Format string bugs can be eliminated by banning non-literal formats in code review and static analysis.
gettext-style localisation can reintroduce the problem if translated strings are treated as trusted code.
pitfalls: Writing printf(input) because the string happens to be a log message today.
Assuming that because the binary is compiled with FORTIFY_SOURCE, %n is always blocked.

code.issue: The first call parses user_input as a format string, so conversions consume missing arguments and %n can write. The second fixes the format and passes the text as an argument.

mcqs.question: Why is %n especially dangerous in a format string vulnerability?
options: It reads a string from an arbitrary address
It writes the number of characters printed so far through a pointer from the argument list
It terminates the process immediately
It disables stack canaries
mcqs.rationale: %n performs a write rather than a read. With attacker-controlled conversions, the pointer comes from the stack or from data the attacker placed there, giving a memory write primitive.

facts.title: Use-after-free turns a stale pointer into attacker-influenced data
facts.fact: free releases an allocation but does not change the pointer that referred to it, so any later read or write through that pointer is undefined behaviour and may touch memory that has been reused for a different object. A double free corrupts the allocator's free lists and is a common path to arbitrary write in older allocators. The ownership rule is simple: one component frees, and every other holder is invalidated at that moment; setting the pointer to NULL after free prevents a second free but does not fix other aliases.
details: free(NULL) is defined and does nothing, which is why assigning NULL after free is a useful local habit.
A pointer copied into another structure is a second owner unless the design says otherwise.
AddressSanitizer's use-after-free detection quarantines freed memory so stale accesses are reported.
Dangling pointers in long-lived caches are especially dangerous because the memory may be reused by attacker-controlled data.
Reference counting and arena ownership make lifetime explicit, at the cost of discipline or performance.
Double free through two different aliases is not prevented by checking one of them for NULL.
pitfalls: Returning a pointer to a local buffer or to memory that the function has already freed.
Using a pointer after realloc, which may have moved and freed the original block.

code.issue: The first function returns a pointer that it has already freed, so the caller reads freed memory. The second transfers ownership to the caller, which must free the result.

mcqs.question: After free(p), which statement is guaranteed by the C standard?
options: p becomes NULL automatically
The memory is zeroed
p still holds the old address, and using it is undefined behaviour
The allocator returns the same block on the next malloc
mcqs.rationale: free takes the pointer by value and cannot change the caller's variable. The address remains in p, the memory may be reused, and any dereference is undefined behaviour.

facts.title: Canaries, PIE, RELRO, and sanitizers address different failure modes
facts.fact: Stack canaries place a checked value between local buffers and the saved return address, so a linear overflow is detected on function return; -fstack-protector-strong covers functions with arrays or address-taken locals. PIE plus ASLR randomises the load address of the executable and libraries, RELRO with -z now makes the GOT read-only after relocation, and NX marks writable pages non-executable. FORTIFY_SOURCE adds checked variants of libc functions when the object size is known. Sanitizers such as ASan and UBSan are development tools that detect the bug rather than a production hardening layer, and none of these controls stops a logic bug that never corrupts control data.
details: Canaries detect overwrites on return; they do not prevent the write and do not protect heap objects.
Full RELRO requires -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now; partial RELRO leaves the GOT writable during lazy binding.
PIE must be linked with -pie, not only compiled with -fPIE, for the executable itself to be randomised.
FORTIFY_SOURCE needs optimisation enabled and a libc built with support; it is not a language guarantee.
ASan and UBSan should run in CI with representative inputs, because they only report paths that execute.
Control-flow integrity and shadow stacks address return-oriented programming, which canaries alone do not.
pitfalls: Believing ASLR makes an overflow unexploitable; an information leak can defeat it.
Shipping a binary built with -fsanitize=address and treating the sanitizer as production hardening.

commands.purpose: Build with the common hardening set: fortify, canaries, PIE, and full RELRO.
Confirm the executable is ET_DYN (PIE) rather than ET_EXEC.
Check that a RELRO segment is present in the linked binary.
Build a development binary that reports memory and undefined-behaviour errors.

misconceptions.claim: A binary with canaries and ASLR cannot be exploited through a buffer overflow.
misconceptions.correction: Canaries catch some return-address overwrites and ASLR raises the cost of code reuse, but an info leak, a heap target, or a non-return control flow can bypass both. Hardening reduces impact; it does not make the bug safe.

facts.title: Complexity describes growth, and the constant matters at real input sizes
facts.fact: Big-O notation describes how an algorithm's work grows as the input grows, ignoring constant factors: a loop over n values is O(n), a nested loop over the same values is O(n^2), and a hash lookup is O(1) on average but O(n) in the worst case when every key collides. Two O(n log n) implementations can differ by a large constant, so complexity ranks algorithms but does not replace measurement. Estimate the input size the code will actually see, then measure with representative data before optimising.
details: Slicing a list inside a loop copies elements and can turn an apparently linear scan into quadratic time and memory churn.
A set membership test is average O(1); a list membership test is O(n), which matters inside request handlers.
Sorting is O(n log n) comparison-based; repeated membership checks after sorting cost O(log n) each.
Logarithmic factors are easy to miss: a heap operation is O(log n), so n insertions are O(n log n).
Amortised analysis explains why appending to a dynamic array is O(1) on average despite occasional reallocation.
Measure with a profiler rather than guessing which line dominates.
pitfalls: Assuming an O(1) operation is always faster than an O(log n) one, regardless of constants.
Optimising a function that is called once while leaving a hot inner loop quadratic.

mcqs.question: An algorithm performs a list membership test for each of n items. What is its expected time complexity?
options: O(log n)
O(n)
mcqs.rationale: Each membership test scans up to n elements, and it is performed n times, giving O(n^2). Using a set for the lookups would reduce the expected cost to O(n).

facts.title: Read a traceback from the innermost frame outward, and separate cause from symptom
facts.fact: A Python traceback lists the call chain in the order the calls were made, so the frame nearest the bottom is where the exception was raised and the frames above show how execution arrived there. The final line names the exception type and message; when exceptions are chained, the section after 'The above exception was the direct cause' or 'During handling of the above exception' is a separate failure that must be read on its own. Fix the innermost cause first, because outer frames often only report where a bad value was used.
details: The caret markers under a line in Python 3.11 and later point at the exact expression that failed.
A KeyError names the missing key; a TypeError names the operation and the types it received.
Exception chaining with raise ... from ... preserves the original cause and is preferable to a bare re-raise with a new message.
The deepest frame is not always the bug: a validation error raised at the bottom may be caused by bad data accepted at the top.
Reproduce with the smallest input that still fails, then add a regression test before changing behaviour.
Log the traceback at the boundary where the request is handled, not at every layer.
pitfalls: Reading only the last line and patching the symptom without the frame that supplied the bad value.
Catching an exception and raising a new one without chaining, which destroys the original traceback.

logs.text:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/srv/app/api.py", line 42, in handler
    report = build_report(order_id)
  File "/srv/app/reports.py", line 17, in build_report
    return store.fetch(order_id)
  File "/srv/app/store.py", line 88, in fetch
    return self._cache[key]
KeyError: 'ord-1042'
logs.reading: The exception was raised in store.fetch at line 88 when the cache lookup missed; handler and build_report are the call chain, not the defect. The missing key is the order identifier, so the next question is why the cache and the datastore disagree, not why api.py raised.

mcqs.question: In a standard Python traceback, which frame is closest to the point where the exception was raised?
options: The first frame after the header
The last frame before the exception line
The frame named in the exception message
The outermost frame in the application
mcqs.rationale: Frames are printed in call order, so the bottom frame is where the failing operation executed. The exception line after it reports the type and message.

facts.title: Safe, idempotent, and cacheable are different HTTP method properties
facts.fact: A method is safe when the client does not request a state change, and idempotent when repeating the same request has the same intended effect as sending it once. GET and HEAD are safe and idempotent; PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe; POST is neither, so retrying it automatically can duplicate an order or a payment. Status codes carry semantics too: 401 means authentication is missing or invalid and invites a credential challenge, 403 means the identity is known but not permitted, and 404 versus 500 distinguishes a missing resource from a server fault.
details: An idempotency key lets a client retry a POST safely by making the server recognise the repeated attempt.
A 5xx response says the server failed, not that the request was invalid; automatic retries need backoff and a cap.
GET responses can be cached and retried freely only when the representation is not sensitive and the request has no side effects.
405 Method Not Allowed must include an Allow header listing the supported methods.
301, 302, and 303 commonly turn a POST into a GET; 307 and 308 preserve the method and body across the redirect.
Returning 200 with an error body hides failures from clients, retries, and monitoring.
pitfalls: Retrying a POST on timeout without an idempotency mechanism.
Using 403 when the real problem is a missing or expired credential, which prevents the client from re-authenticating.

mcqs.question: Which method is idempotent but not safe?
options: GET
HEAD
PUT
POST
mcqs.rationale: PUT replaces a resource, so repeating it has the same effect, but it does change state and is therefore not safe. POST is neither safe nor idempotent in general.

facts.title: Nested quantifiers can make a backtracking regex take exponential time
facts.fact: A backtracking engine tries alternatives depth-first, so a pattern with nested repetition such as (\w+\s?)+ can re-partition the same input in exponentially many ways when the overall match fails. Anchors constrain where a match can start but do not remove the internal ambiguity; a pattern with two adjacent unbounded repetitions over overlapping character sets, like ^(a+)+$, is the classic case. Rewrite the pattern so each character is matched by exactly one repetition, or use a linear-time engine or a timeout when the pattern must accept hostile input.
details: Greedy and lazy quantifiers change which match is found first, not the worst-case backtracking behaviour.
fullmatch and a trailing $ are not equivalent in every engine; choose one anchoring strategy deliberately.
Possessive quantifiers and atomic groups (where supported) prevent the engine from re-entering a repetition.
Python 3.11 added atomic groups and possessive quantifiers to re; older versions need a rewrite.
Measure with adversarial input lengths, because a pattern can be fast on normal data and quadratic on crafted data.
Input length limits are a cheap backstop when the regex engine has no timeout.
pitfalls: Testing only valid inputs, which match early and never exercise the failing backtracking path.
Assuming an anchored pattern is linear because it starts with ^.

code.vulnerable:
import re

NAME = re.compile(r"^(\w+\s?)+$")


def valid_name(value: str) -> bool:
    return NAME.fullmatch(value) is not None
code.secure:
import re

NAME = re.compile(r"^\w+(?: \w+)*$")


def valid_name(value: str) -> bool:
    return NAME.fullmatch(value) is not None
code.issue: The nested repetition lets the engine split the same characters in many ways, so a failing long input explores exponentially many paths. The rewritten pattern makes each space a required separator, removing the ambiguity.

mcqs.question: Which pattern is most likely to exhibit catastrophic backtracking on a non-matching input?
mcqs.rationale: The inner a+ and outer + can partition a run of a's in exponentially many ways when the final anchor fails. The other patterns have no nested repetition over the same characters.

facts.title: Characters, code points, UTF-16 units, and bytes are four different counts
facts.fact: Text has to be encoded before it becomes bytes: UTF-8 stores a code point in one to four bytes, UTF-16 stores it in one or two 16-bit units, and JavaScript's string length counts UTF-16 units while Python's len counts code points. Slicing or truncating at an arbitrary byte or unit boundary can split a character and produce invalid output. Percent-encoding and base64 are transport encodings with different purposes: percent-encoding makes bytes safe inside a URI component, while base64 makes arbitrary bytes safe in a text channel and adds about a third to the size. Neither provides confidentiality.
details: An emoji outside the Basic Multilingual Plane is two UTF-16 units, so JavaScript length is 2 for one visible character.
Decoding with errors='ignore' silently drops bytes; errors='replace' substitutes a marker; strict raises.
Base64 of UTF-8 text is not the same string as base64 of UTF-16 text, which is a common interoperability bug.
Percent-encoding operates on UTF-8 bytes in modern URIs; decoding twice can turn %2520 into a space.
Normalisation (NFC/NFD) affects equality and length; compare normalised forms when the source is uncontrolled.
HTTP headers are historically byte-oriented; the charset belongs in Content-Type for the body, not in a guess.
pitfalls: Using len(text) as a byte count when writing to a fixed-width field or a Content-Length header.
Treating base64 as encryption or as a way to make input safe for SQL or HTML.

code.vulnerable:
def header(title: str) -> bytes:
    return ("== " + title + " ==").encode("utf-8")[:40]
code.issue: The first version slices raw bytes at a fixed offset and can cut a multi-byte character in half. The second decodes the prefix with an error policy before re-encoding, so the output stays valid UTF-8.

mcqs.question: A JavaScript string contains one emoji outside the Basic Multilingual Plane. What does its .length property report?
options: It depends on the file encoding
mcqs.rationale: JavaScript strings are sequences of UTF-16 code units, and such a code point is represented by a surrogate pair, so length is 2. Python's len on the equivalent str would be 1.

facts.title: A read-modify-write sequence needs mutual exclusion or an atomic operation
facts.fact: Two threads that each read a counter, add one, and write it back can both read the same old value, so one increment is lost even though both operations completed. The problem is the gap between read and write, not the individual operations, and it appears in databases, file updates, and in-memory caches as well as in threads. A lock around the whole sequence restores correctness; an atomic compare-and-swap achieves it without a lock; a database transaction with the right isolation level or a conditional UPDATE does the same at the storage layer.
details: Locks must cover every access path, including reads used for decisions, or the race simply moves.
Check-then-act across a filesystem boundary is a time-of-check to time-of-use race; use an exclusive create or rename.
Threading bugs often disappear under a debugger because it changes timing; stress tests and race detectors are more reliable.
Python's GIL does not make multi-step operations atomic; it only prevents simultaneous bytecode execution.
In asyncio, an await between read and write is enough to interleave another task.
Prefer immutable data and message passing where the design allows it, because shared mutable state is the root cause.
pitfalls: Assuming a single-threaded event loop removes races, when awaits yield control between steps.
Testing concurrency only with a loop count of one, where no interleaving occurs.

code.issue: The read and the write are separate steps, so two threads can both observe the same value and overwrite each other. The lock makes the whole sequence exclusive.

mcqs.question: Two threads run value = value + 1 concurrently and the final value is one less than expected. What happened?
options: The addition overflowed
Both threads read the same old value before either wrote, so one update was lost
The GIL serialised the writes incorrectly
The variable was cached in a register per thread permanently
mcqs.rationale: The read-modify-write is not atomic. Interleaving read, read, write, write loses one increment, which is why the sequence needs a lock or an atomic operation.

references.title: CWE-362: Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization

facts.title: A regression test should fail before the fix and pass after it
facts.fact: A test that passes both before and after a change proves nothing about the change, so the disciplined sequence is to reproduce the defect with the smallest input, watch the new test fail, then fix the cause and watch it pass. Unit tests pin specific behaviour, property-based tests generate inputs and check invariants, and fuzzers search for crashes or hangs over a large input space. Flaky tests are usually evidence of hidden state, timing, or ordering assumptions, so quarantine and diagnose them instead of rerunning until green.
details: A property such as 'encoding then decoding returns the original value' covers inputs a hand-written case list will miss.
Fuzzing needs a seed and a corpus committed with the finding so the failure is reproducible.
Assert on observable behaviour rather than internal call order, or refactoring will break the suite for no reason.
A test that depends on the current time, network, or test order is a flake waiting to happen.
Mutation testing checks whether the tests detect small changes to the code, which measures assertion strength.
Negative tests matter: invalid input, empty collections, and permission failures are where many defects live.
pitfalls: Writing the fix first and then a test that asserts whatever the new code happens to do.
Marking a flaky test as skipped permanently instead of finding the shared state behind it.

commands.purpose: Run the test suite with concise output.
Run a single focused test while reproducing a defect.
Re-run only the tests that failed on the previous run.

misconceptions.claim: High test coverage means the code is well tested.
misconceptions.correction: Coverage measures which lines executed, not which behaviours were asserted. A suite can execute every line and still miss boundary conditions, error paths, and concurrency interleavings.

facts.title: Bisect the problem space and keep a written hypothesis
facts.fact: Debugging is search, so the efficient move is to halve the space at each step: confirm which layer produces the bad value, which input first triggers it, and which change introduced it. Write down the hypothesis and the observation that would falsify it before running an experiment, because otherwise each run becomes a guess. Reduce the reproduction to the smallest case that still fails, then fix the cause and re-run the original case; if the small case stops failing but the original does not, the reduction removed a second factor.
details: Binary search over commits, configuration flags, or input size finds the boundary faster than reading code.
Print or log the actual values at the boundary instead of reasoning about what they should be.
A failing case that disappears when logging is added usually indicates a timing or state bug.
Change one variable per experiment; two simultaneous changes make the result uninterpretable.
Keep the reduced reproduction as a regression test so the same bug cannot return silently.
Check the assumptions you have not verified: which binary is running, which config file was loaded, which database was contacted.
pitfalls: Changing several things at once and concluding the last one fixed it.
Trusting a stale build or a cached dependency while debugging source code.

commands.purpose: Start an interactive debugger at the first line to inspect state while stepping.
Run with development-mode warnings enabled so resource and deprecation issues surface.

mcqs.question: A bug disappears when you add logging near the suspected code. What is the most useful next step?
options: Keep the logging and close the issue
Suspect a timing, ordering, or shared-state dependency and test that hypothesis
Assume the logger fixed the race condition
Increase the log level everywhere
mcqs.rationale: Logging changes timing and can hide an interleaving. The observation points to concurrency or hidden state, so the next experiment should control or instrument that timing rather than treat the symptom as resolved.
